q: According to §1 of the Organon, the physician's high and only mission is:
opts: to construct theories about the inner nature of disease
to explain the phenomena of life and disease
to prove medicines on healthy persons
to restore the sick to health, to cure
why: §1: the physician's high and only mission is to restore the sick to health, to cure, as it is termed; not to spin speculative systems.

q: According to §2, the highest ideal of cure is:
opts: removal of the most troublesome symptom as quickly as possible
palliation of suffering until the disease runs its natural course
removal of the material cause of disease by evacuation
rapid, gentle and permanent restoration of health on easily comprehensible principles
why: §2 defines the ideal cure as rapid, gentle and permanent restoration of health, or removal of the disease in its whole extent, in the shortest, most reliable and most harmless way.

q: According to §5, in an acute disease the physician is helped in curing by knowing:
opts: the family history of chronic disease
the patient's constitution and temperament only
why: §5: the exciting cause helps in acute disease, while the fundamental cause (usually a chronic miasm) is sought from the history of chronic disease.

q: According to §10, the material organism without the vital force is:
opts: still able to react to medicines, though weakly
governed by the chemical and physical laws of life
capable of sensation but not of self-preservation
capable of no sensation, no function and no self-preservation
why: §10: without the vital force the organism is dead; all sensation and function come from the immaterial vital principle.

q: According to §§31 and 32, medicines differ from natural disease-causing agents because medicines:
opts: act only when the person is sufficiently susceptible
act unconditionally, on every living person at all times
act only on the diseased part of the body
why: §31: natural morbific agents act only conditionally, when the organism is susceptible; §32: true medicines act at all times, under all circumstances, on every living body.

q: According to §27, the curative power of medicines depends on their symptoms being:
opts: opposite to the disease and equal in strength
similar to the disease but weaker than it
identical to the disease in every respect
similar to the disease but stronger than it
why: §27: the curative power of medicines depends on symptoms similar to the disease but superior to it in strength.

q: When a new dissimilar disease has acted on the organism for long and joins the old one, each occupying its own region, Hahnemann (§40) calls the result:
why: §40: dissimilar diseases may unite into a complex disease, each occupying its own locality in the organism; allopathic drugging commonly produces this.

q: According to §71, the three points necessary for cure are knowledge of:
opts: the cause, the pathology and the prognosis of disease
the disease, the powers of medicines, and how to apply them
the miasm, the temperament and the diathesis
the diet, the regimen and the environment
why: §71: the physician must learn what is to be cured in disease, the pathogenetic powers of medicines, and the mode of employing them.

q: Diseases such as smallpox, measles and whooping cough, which recur in the same manner and attack a person usually only once in life, are called in §73:
why: §73 groups acute diseases into individual, sporadic, epidemic and acute miasms; smallpox and measles are acute miasms of fixed character.

q: According to §§74 and 75, the most deplorable and incurable of all chronic diseases are those produced by:
why: §75: artificial chronic diseases caused by allopathic treatment are the most deplorable and incurable of all.

q: In case taking (§84), while the patient narrates his sufferings the physician should:
opts: guide the narration with questions from the start
note only the symptoms that fit the diagnosis
ask the relatives first and then the patient
keep silent and not interrupt, noting everything in the patient's own words
why: §84: the physician lets the patient and friends say all they have to say without interruption and writes it down in their very expressions.

q: According to §85, while recording the case the physician should:
opts: group the symptoms under the diagnosis
write the symptoms in order of their severity
begin a fresh line with every new symptom, so each stands separately
record only the symptoms that seem important
why: §85: a fresh line for each new circumstance, symptoms ranged separately one below the other, so each can be completed later.

q: In a chronic case where the patient has been taking medicines up to the time of the visit, §91 advises the physician to:
opts: record the case at once, as the drug symptoms are part of the disease
continue the old medicines and add the homoeopathic remedy
leave him some days without medicine before taking the final picture
antidote the old medicines immediately with Nux vomica
why: §91: symptoms during a course of medicine do not give the pure picture; in chronic cases the patient may be left a few days without medicine.

q: In chronic diseases (§94), the physician must specially enquire into the patient's:
opts: occupation, mode of living, diet and domestic situation
why: §94: in chronic cases the circumstances of the patient's daily life are noted to find what causes or maintains the disease.

q: According to §99, investigating the case is generally easier in acute than in chronic disease because:
opts: acute diseases have fewer symptoms in every case
acute diseases do not need individualisation
all the phenomena are recent and still fresh in the patient's memory
why: §99: in acute disease the symptoms are recent and striking, so the investigation is easier and quicker.

q: According to §108, the peculiar effects of medicines on human health can be ascertained only by:
opts: giving them experimentally in moderate doses to healthy persons
observing their effects in the sick
chemical analysis of the drug substance
why: §108: there is no other way than to administer medicines experimentally to healthy persons.

q: Hahnemann held (§119) that one medicine can never be a substitute (succedaneum) for another because:
opts: medicines from the same family act alike
only the dose decides the action
substitutes are forbidden by the law of potency
every medicine has its own peculiar and distinct action
why: §119: as every plant species differs, each medicine has a distinct action, so none can replace another.

q: According to §127, medicines should be proved on:
opts: males only, to avoid confusion with menstrual symptoms
children, as they are most sensitive
the sick, as they react more clearly
why: §127: medicines must be tested on both sexes, also to reveal the changes they produce in the sexual sphere.

q: According to §138, the changes of health that a prover feels during the action of the medicine are:
opts: to be regarded as derived solely from that medicine
to be ignored unless they are new to him
to be regarded as his own latent disease
to be recorded only if confirmed in animals
why: §138: all sufferings and changes during the proving, under proper conditions, belong to the medicine and are recorded as its symptoms.

q: According to §141, the best of all provings are those made by:
opts: the healthy, unprejudiced and sensitive physician on himself
students under the supervision of a professor
volunteers who know nothing of the drug
why: §141: the best pure experiments are those the healthy, unprejudiced, sensitive physician makes on himself.

q: A slight aggravation in the first hours after a well-chosen remedy in an acute disease is, according to §§157 and 158:
opts: a good sign that the disease will probably yield to the first dose
a sign that the remedy was wrong and must be antidoted
a sign that the dose should be repeated at once
a sign that the case is incurable
why: §158: the slight homoeopathic aggravation in the first hours is a very good prognostic that the acute disease will yield to the first dose.

q: According to §159, the smaller the dose of the homoeopathic remedy:
opts: the smaller and shorter is the homoeopathic aggravation
the longer the remedy must be repeated
the greater the risk of new symptoms
why: §159: the smaller the dose, the smaller and shorter the apparent increase of the disease in the first hours.

q: According to §201, in chronic disease the vital force develops a local malady on an external part in order to:
opts: draw attention to the internal organ affected
quiet or silence the internal disease
why: §201: the vital force produces and keeps up a local symptom on a part not vital to life, to silence the internal disease; removing it externally is harmful.

q: According to §213, a cure in conformity with nature is impossible unless the physician observes:
opts: the changes in the blood and urine
the pathological changes in the tissues
the changes in the mind and disposition of the patient
why: §213: we shall never cure conformably to nature unless we attend to the changes in the mind and disposition in every disease.

q: According to §215, almost all so-called mental and emotional diseases are:
opts: bodily diseases in which the mental symptoms have increased while the bodily symptoms have declined
purely spiritual diseases that need no medicine
diseases caused only by emotional shocks
local diseases of the brain substance
why: §215: mental diseases are corporeal diseases in which the derangement of mind and disposition has become predominant, like a one-sided disease.

q: In acute diseases (§§262 and 263), the patient's craving for particular food and drink should generally be:
opts: gratified within reason, as it comes from the instinct of the vital force
strictly refused, as it may antidote the remedy
replaced by a fixed hospital diet
satisfied only after the fever subsides
why: §262–263: in acute disease the desires of the patient, guided by the vital force, should not be opposed, though a slight gratification of palliative wishes is enough.

q: The aphorism that states that in no case is it necessary, and therefore not permissible, to give the patient more than one single simple medicine at a time is:
why: §273 states the rule of the single remedy (simplex); §§272 to 274 deal with it.

q: According to §279, the dose of the correctly chosen homoeopathic remedy:
opts: must be large enough to produce an aggravation
must be increased daily until improvement begins
can never be made so small that it is not stronger than the natural disease
is unimportant if the remedy is similar
why: §279: the dose of the homoeopathic remedy can never be prepared so small that it is not stronger than the natural disease it can cure.

q: Besides the tongue, mouth and stomach, §284 says medicines can act through:
opts: olfaction and inhalation, and through the skin
why: §284: the nose and respiratory organs (by olfaction and inhalation) and the skin can also receive the action of medicines.

q: In Kent's first observation, a prolonged aggravation followed by a final decline of the patient means:
opts: the remedy was correct and cure will follow
the remedy was only a palliative
the patient was incurable and the remedy acted too deeply on a weakened vitality
the patient is oversensitive and proves every remedy
why: Kent (Lectures on Homoeopathic Philosophy): prolonged aggravation with decline shows an incurable patient; the deep antipsoric set up destructive changes.

q: In Kent's fourth observation, recovery of the patient with no aggravation whatever indicates:
opts: a wrong remedy that has acted by chance
no organic disease, with the remedy and potency well suited
why: Kent: cure without any aggravation means there was no organic disease and the remedy was exactly similar in a suitable potency.

q: In Kent's sixth observation, too short a relief of symptoms after a remedy points to:
opts: organic (structural) changes or something interfering with the remedy
a remedy that was too deep for the case
why: Kent: amelioration that lasts too short a time suggests structural change in the organs, or in acute cases a rapidly advancing process.

q: In Kent's eighth observation, patients who prove every remedy they receive are:
opts: oversensitive, idiosyncratic patients who are often incurable
patients who need repeated high doses
patients with a purely acute disease
why: Kent: some patients prove every remedy; they are oversensitive and idiosyncratic, and such cases are often incurable; lower potencies are used.

q: According to Kent's ninth observation, what does a well-conducted proving generally do to a healthy prover?
opts: It makes the prover more susceptible to all diseases
It has no effect when high potencies are used
why: Kent's ninth observation: provers in good health are usually benefited, and sensitive provers may even be cured of latent troubles, by careful provings.

q: According to Kent, if the first prescription has produced no action at all, the next prescription is:
opts: always a repetition of the same remedy in a higher potency
not a second prescription, but really a first prescription again
why: Kent: the second prescription is the one that follows a prescription that has acted; if the first did nothing, the next is still a first prescription.

q: Kent, following Swedenborg, described the vital force as:
why: Kent's Lectures on Homoeopathic Philosophy call the vital force 'simple substance', an immaterial substance with formative intelligence.

q: Kent traced the origin of psora to:
opts: disordered willing and thinking of man, a spiritual sickness that came before the itch
infection by the itch mite alone
why: Kent (Lectures on Homoeopathic Philosophy) held psora to be the primitive disorder of the human race, arising from man's wrong willing and thinking.

q: In 'The Genius of Homoeopathy', Stuart Close defined susceptibility as:
opts: the tendency of a disease to spread in a community
the power of a drug to produce symptoms in the healthy
the general quality of the living organism of receiving impressions, the power to react to stimuli
the strength of the medicine after potentisation
why: Close: susceptibility is the capability of the living organism to receive impressions and react to stimuli; it governs both cure and the choice of dose.

q: 'The Principles and Art of Cure by Homoeopathy' was written by:
why: Herbert A. Roberts published 'The Principles and Art of Cure by Homoeopathy' in 1936.

q: The repertory 'Sensations As If' was compiled by:
why: H. A. Roberts compiled 'Sensations As If' (1937), a repertory of the 'as if' sensations.

q: Samuel Hahnemann was born in 1755 at:
why: Hahnemann was born on 10 April 1755 at Meissen, Saxony; he graduated MD from Erlangen in 1779 and later lived at Leipzig and Köthen.

q: Hahnemann's 'Essay on a New Principle for Ascertaining the Curative Powers of Drugs' (1796) appeared in:
opts: the Archiv für die homöopathische Heilkunst
why: The 1796 essay, regarded as the formal birth of homoeopathy, was published in Hufeland's Journal.

q: The term 'allopathy' was coined by:
why: Hahnemann coined 'allopathy' for the system that treats with medicines producing effects different from the disease.

q: Boenninghausen's 'complete symptom' consists of:
why: Boenninghausen's concept of the complete symptom has four parts: location, sensation, modalities and concomitants.

q: In selecting the homoeopathic remedy, which symptoms are of the least value?
opts: Common pathognomonic symptoms of the disease
Physical generals such as thermal reaction
why: Pathognomonic symptoms belong to the disease, not the individual, so they rank lowest for remedy selection (§153, Kent).

q: Hahnemann's chief remedy for syphilis was:
why: In 'The Chronic Diseases' Hahnemann treated syphilis with Mercurius; Thuja and Nitric acid were his remedies for sycosis and Sulphur for psora.

q: Suspicion, secretiveness, jealousy and fixed ideas are the mental features of which miasm?
why: Sycotic mentals are suspicious, secretive, jealous and fixed in ideas; psora is anxious and fearful, syphilis destructive and depressed.

q: Deep depression with suicidal thoughts, mental dullness and destructive impulses are the mental features of which miasm?
why: The syphilitic miasm is destructive both in tissue and mind: depression, dullness, suicidal and destructive tendencies.

q: A thin child with recurrent colds, enlarged glands, emaciation despite a good appetite, a changeable mind and a desire to travel shows the features of:
why: The tubercular diathesis shows emaciation with appetite, recurrent respiratory infections, glands, dissatisfaction and a desire for change and travel.

q: According to J. H. Allen, the tubercular diathesis (pseudo-psora) is a combination of:
opts: all three miasms in equal parts
why: J. H. Allen in 'The Chronic Miasms' regarded pseudo-psora (the tubercular diathesis) as a mixed miasm of psora and syphilis.

q: Hahnemann stated in 'The Chronic Diseases' that, the chronic miasm that has produced by far the fewest chronic diseases is:
why: Hahnemann called sycosis the miasm that has produced by far the fewest chronic diseases, psora being the source of the great majority.

q: 'The Chronic Miasms' (Psora and Pseudo-psora; Sycosis) was written by:
why: John Henry Allen wrote 'The Chronic Miasms'; H. C. Allen wrote the Keynotes and T. F. Allen the Encyclopedia of Pure Materia Medica.

q: Long before Hahnemann, the idea that disease may be cured by similars was mentioned by:
why: Hippocrates recognised both contraries and similars as ways of cure; Galen built his system on contraries.

q: The Arndt-Schulz law, quoted in support of the minimum dose, states that:
opts: the effect of a drug is directly proportional to its dose
weak stimuli excite vital activity, moderate ones favour it, strong ones retard it and very strong ones arrest it
every drug has only one action at all doses
the smaller the dose the stronger the toxic effect
why: The Arndt-Schulz law describes the opposite actions of small and large stimuli, used to explain the minimum dose.

q: Hahnemann described the vital force as acting:
opts: only under the control of the physician
automatically and instinctively, without reason or judgement
why: In the Organon (introduction and §22), the vital force is called instinctive, unintelligent and automatic; it cannot cure chronic disease by itself.

q: Hahnemann's 'Materia Medica Pura' was published in:
why: Materia Medica Pura (Reine Arzneimittellehre) appeared in six volumes from 1811 to 1821; the ten-volume work of 1874–79 is T. F. Allen's Encyclopedia.

q: Hahnemann's 'Fragmenta de viribus medicamentorum positivis' (1805), the first collection of provings, contained:
why: Fragmenta de viribus (1805), written in Latin, recorded the provings of 27 drugs.

q: 'The Encyclopedia of Pure Materia Medica' in ten volumes was compiled by:
why: Timothy Field Allen compiled the 10-volume Encyclopedia of Pure Materia Medica (1874–1879), a schematic pure Materia Medica.

q: 'A Dictionary of Practical Materia Medica' in three volumes was written by:
why: John Henry Clarke wrote the three-volume Dictionary of Practical Materia Medica.

q: 'Leaders in Homoeopathic Therapeutics' was written by:
why: E. B. Nash's 'Leaders in Homoeopathic Therapeutics' gives the leading symptoms of remedies with comparisons.

q: 'Homoeopathic Drug Pictures' was written by:
why: Margaret Tyler's 'Homoeopathic Drug Pictures' presents remedies as living portraits, drawing on Kent and others.

q: 'Relationship of Remedies and Sides of the Body', a standard reference on complementary and inimical remedies, was written by:
why: R. Gibson Miller's small book lists the complementary, inimical, antidotal and following remedies, and the sides of the body each affects.

q: The idea of the 'keynote', a striking characteristic that leads to the remedy, is credited to:
why: Henry N. Guernsey introduced the keynote approach; H. C. Allen later developed it in his 'Keynotes'.

q: In Materia Medica, a 'modality' is:
opts: the sensation felt by the patient
the pathological diagnosis of the disease
a condition that makes a symptom better or worse
why: A modality is any circumstance (time, temperature, motion, position, food, weather) that ameliorates or aggravates a symptom.

q: Camphor is known in homoeopathy as an antidote to:
why: Camphor antidotes the action of most vegetable remedies, so it is kept away from patients under treatment.

q: Hepar sulphuris is well known as an antidote to the ill effects of:
why: Hepar sulph (with Nitric acid) is the classic antidote to the abuse of mercury.

q: Which remedy is inimical to Mercurius and should not follow it?
why: Boericke lists Silicea as incompatible with Mercurius; Hepar is its antidote.

q: Ammonium carbonicum is inimical to:
why: Boericke: Ammonium carbonicum is inimical to Lachesis.

q: Which remedy is regarded as the chronic of Belladonna?
why: Calcarea carb is the chronic complement of Belladonna; Sulphur is the chronic of Aconite and Natrum mur of Ignatia.

q: Which remedy is the chronic complement of Bryonia?
why: Boericke gives Alumina (and Rhus tox) as complementary to Bryonia; Alumina is called its chronic.

q: Which remedy is regarded as the chronic of Apis mellifica?
why: Natrum muriaticum is the chronic of Apis, as it is of Ignatia.

q: Sulphur is listed as complementary to which remedy for rectal complaints and diarrhoea?
why: Boericke: Aloe – complementary Sulphur; and Sulphur's complementaries include Aloe and Psorinum.

q: The concept of organ remedies (organopathy), derived from Rademacher, was developed in homoeopathy chiefly by:
why: J. Compton Burnett popularised organ remedies, such as Ceanothus for the spleen and Chelidonium for the liver, building on Rademacher.

q: Aconitum napellus is commonly known as:
why: Aconitum napellus (Ranunculaceae) is monkshood or wolf's bane; deadly nightshade is Belladonna, foxglove Digitalis and thorn apple Stramonium.

q: Aethusa cynapium is commonly known as:
why: Aethusa cynapium is fool's parsley (Umbelliferae); wind flower is Pulsatilla, poison nut Nux vomica and bitter-sweet Dulcamara.

q: A sense of insecurity in the rectum, with stool escaping when passing flatus and lumps of jelly-like mucus, is characteristic of:
why: Aloe: insecurity of the rectum, stool passes with flatus, jelly-like mucous lumps (Allen's Keynotes, Boericke).

q: Fear of being touched or approached, and a hot head with a cool body, are characteristic of:
why: Arnica fears touch or the approach of anyone; Boericke notes head hot, body cool.

q: In a typhoid state, the patient can swallow only liquids, as the least solid food causes gagging; the remedy is:
why: Baptisia: painless sore throat, can swallow liquids only, the least solid food gags (Boericke, Allen).

q: Sudden high fever with burning, radiating heat felt by the hand, a bright red face, dilated pupils and throbbing carotids calls for:
why: Belladonna: suddenness, intense dry heat, redness, throbbing and dilated pupils; Aconite lacks the throbbing congestion and has fear and restlessness.

q: A bubbling sensation in the kidney region, with pains that radiate from the kidney in all directions, is characteristic of:
why: Berberis vulgaris (barberry): radiating renal pains and a bubbling sensation in the kidneys (Boericke).

q: In delirium the patient talks of his business and wants to go home, although he is at home. The remedy is:
why: Bryonia: delirious, talks about business, wants to go home (Boericke, Allen's Keynotes).

q: Chamomilla (Matricaria chamomilla) belongs to which plant family?
why: Chamomilla, like Arnica, belongs to the Compositae; Belladonna is Solanaceae, Aconite Ranunculaceae and Nux vomica Loganiaceae.

q: Distension of the whole abdomen with flatulence that is not relieved by belching or passing flatus is characteristic of:
why: China: the whole abdomen is tympanitic and eructation gives no relief; Carbo veg is upper abdomen, relieved by belching; Lycopodium is lower abdomen.

q: Nausea, even to fainting, from the smell of cooking food, especially fish or eggs, is a keynote of:
why: Colchicum: the smell of food cooking causes nausea to the point of fainting (Allen's Keynotes); it is also a gout remedy.

q: Digitalis purpurea is prepared from the plant commonly called:
why: Digitalis is foxglove; monkshood is Aconite, henbane Hyoscyamus and meadow saffron Colchicum.

q: Aching in the bones as if broken, with chill beginning between 7 and 9 a.m. and thirst before the chill, calls for:
why: Eupatorium perfoliatum (boneset): break-bone pains, chill 7–9 a.m., thirst before chill, vomiting of bile (Boericke, Allen).

q: A headache that is relieved by the passing of a profuse quantity of urine is characteristic of:
why: Gelsemium: headache relieved by profuse urination (Allen's Keynotes, Boericke).

q: A dry, spasmodic cough at night that is worse on lying down and relieved by sitting up, in a jealous, suspicious patient, suggests:
why: Hyoscyamus: dry nocturnal cough worse lying down, better sitting up (Boericke).

q: A sore throat that is better from swallowing solid food, a typical paradoxical symptom, is characteristic of:
why: Ignatia, the remedy of contradictions: sore throat relieved by swallowing solids (Boericke, Allen).

q: Profuse, bright red haemorrhage from the uterus or lungs, accompanied by constant nausea, calls for:
why: Ipecac: bright red, profuse, gushing haemorrhage with persistent nausea (Allen's Keynotes).

q: Rheumatism that begins in the feet and travels upwards is characteristic of:
why: Ledum: rheumatism begins in the feet and ascends; Kalmia's pains travel downward (Boericke).

q: Frequent, ineffectual urging for stool in an irritable, sedentary person who lives on stimulants and rich food calls for:
why: Nux vomica: frequent ineffectual urging, passing small quantities, in irritable, zealous, sedentary people; Opium and Alumina have no urging.

q: A fever patient who must be covered in every stage, because he becomes chilly on the slightest uncovering or movement even during the heat, needs:
why: Nux vomica: chilliness in all stages of fever; cannot move or uncover without feeling chilly (Allen's Keynotes).

q: 'The bed feels so hot that she cannot lie on it and keeps moving to find a cool place' is a keynote of:
why: Opium: bed feels so hot she cannot lie on it (Allen's Keynotes); in Arnica and Pyrogen the bed feels too hard.

q: Prolapse of the rectum before or with the stool, with profuse gushing diarrhoea, is characteristic of:
why: Podophyllum: prolapsus ani before or with stool (Boericke, Allen).

q: Pulsatilla nigricans is commonly known as:
why: Pulsatilla nigricans (Ranunculaceae) is the wind flower or pasque flower; marsh tea is Ledum.

q: A red, triangular tip of the tongue is a keynote of:
why: Rhus tox: triangular red tip of the tongue; Veratrum viride has a red streak down the middle.

q: A woman with uterine haemorrhage who finds music intolerable, as it makes her nervous, needs:
why: Sabina (Boericke): music is intolerable and produces nervousness; uterine bleeding with pain from sacrum to pubis.

q: Rheumatism of the right shoulder (deltoid), so that the arm cannot be raised, is characteristic of:
why: Sanguinaria: rheumatism of the right shoulder and deltoid, cannot raise the arm (Boericke).

q: Recurrent styes and chalazia on the eyelids, in a sensitive person with suppressed indignation, call for:
why: Staphisagria: styes and chalazia one after another (Boericke), with the background of suppressed anger.

q: Religious mania with a desire to cut and tear things, and cold sweat on the forehead, points to:
why: Veratrum album: religious mania, destructive impulses to cut and tear, with cold sweat on the forehead (Boericke).

q: Inflammation of the mastoid, with swelling and pain behind the ear, in a fat, chilly, homesick patient, calls for:
why: Capsicum is a classic remedy for mastoiditis (Boericke: swelling and pain behind the ears, inflammation of the mastoid).

q: A suicidal impulse on seeing a knife or blood is characteristic of:
why: Alumina (Boericke): suicidal tendency when seeing a knife or blood.

q: A feeling as if he had two wills, one commanding what the other forbids, is a keynote of:
why: Anacardium: sensation of two wills, with irresistible desire to curse and swear, and the plug sensation.

q: Thick, horny callosities on the soles, split nails and a sentimental mood in the moonlight indicate:
why: Antimonium crudum: horny callosities and warts, cracked nails, sentimental in moonlight (Boericke).

q: Antimonium tartaricum is chemically:
why: Antimonium tartaricum is tartar emetic, the double tartrate of antimony and potassium; Antimonium crudum is the black sulphide.

q: An impulse to jump down when crossing a bridge or standing in a high place calls for:
why: Argentum nitricum: on a high place or bridge, the thought of jumping off; fear of high buildings (Boericke).

q: A fastidious, exacting patient who cannot bear disorder, with burning pains relieved by heat, needs:
why: Arsenicum album is the classic fastidious remedy, with burning pains better by heat and restless anxiety.

q: Caries of the nasal and palatine bones, with ozaena and a putrid smell from the nose, in a depressed syphilitic patient suggests:
why: Aurum met: caries of nasal and palatine bones, ozaena, putrid odour (Boericke), with profound melancholy.

q: A timid child who hides behind furniture when strangers come, and whose tonsils inflame and suppurate with every cold, needs:
why: Baryta carb: bashful child hides behind furniture; quinsy and tonsillitis after every cold (Boericke).

q: Hair that tangles at the tips and sticks together so that it cannot be combed (plica polonica) is a keynote of:
why: Borax: hair frowzy and tangled, splits and sticks together at the tips (Boericke, Allen).

q: Diarrhoea before and during the menses, with the menstrual flow only at night or early morning, is characteristic of:
why: Bovista (Boericke): diarrhoea before and during menses; flow only at night or early in the morning.

q: Fear that she will lose her reason, or that people will notice her confusion, is characteristic of:
why: Calcarea carb: apprehension, fears losing her reason or that people will observe her confusion (Boericke).

q: Headache of schoolchildren, especially girls at puberty, in thin, growing children is characteristic of:
why: Calcarea phos: headache of school girls, with growing pains and slow bone development (Boericke).

q: Burns and scalds with raw, smarting pain, relieved by cold applications, especially before blisters form, call for:
why: Cantharis is the leading remedy for burns and scalds, given before blisters form.

q: Carbo vegetabilis is prepared from:
why: Carbo vegetabilis is wood (vegetable) charcoal; Carbo animalis is animal charcoal, Spongia roasted sponge and Calcarea carb the middle layer of the oyster shell.

q: Involuntary urination in the first sleep at night, and escape of urine on coughing or sneezing, is characteristic of:
why: Causticum: enuresis during first sleep; urine escapes on coughing, sneezing or blowing the nose (Boericke).

q: Anaemia with pallor, in which the face flushes fiery red on the least emotion or exertion (false plethora), calls for:
why: Ferrum met: anaemic yet with false plethora; face flushes red on the least pain, emotion or exertion (Allen's Keynotes).

q: Indifference towards those he loves best, with a buoyant feeling and an increased ability to exert himself without fatigue, suggests:
why: Fluoric acid (Boericke): indifference towards those loved best; increased ability to exercise mentally and physically without fatigue.

q: Eruptions behind the ears and in the bends of the joints that ooze a thick, sticky, honey-like fluid, in an obese, chilly, constipated woman, call for:
why: Graphites: eruptions oozing a thick, honey-like, glutinous fluid, especially behind the ears and in flexures (Allen's Keynotes).

q: Large, knotty stools held together by threads of mucus are characteristic of:
why: Graphites: constipation with large, difficult, knotty stools united by mucous threads (Allen's Keynotes).

q: Weakness and backache, as if the back would break, with sweating, after labour or abortion, call for:
why: Kali carb: backache, sweat and weakness after confinement or miscarriage (Allen's Keynotes, Boericke).

q: A patient who is sensitive to both heat and cold, so that he is called a 'human thermometer', needs:
why: Mercurius: worse from both warmth and cold; a 'human thermometer'.

q: Inability to pass urine in the presence of others is characteristic of:
why: Natrum mur (Allen's Keynotes): cannot pass urine in the presence of others.

q: Mental symptoms with a suicidal impulse following an injury to the head, in a patient worse in damp weather, call for:
why: Natrum sulph: chronic effects of head injuries, mental troubles and suicidal tendency, aggravated by damp (Boericke).

q: Skin eruptions with deep, bleeding cracks that are worse in winter, together with seasickness, point to:
why: Petroleum: deep fissures and cracks worse in winter; nausea from riding in carriages and ships (Boericke).

q: A haughty woman to whom objects around her look small, while she feels physically large, needs:
why: Platina: things look smaller than they are while she feels tall and superior (Boericke).

q: A weak, empty, sinking feeling in the stomach at about 11 a.m. is a keynote of:
why: Sulphur: faint, empty, weak feeling at 11 a.m. (Allen's Keynotes); Natrum mur is worse at 10 a.m.

q: Medorrhinum is prepared from:
opts: the contents of the scabies vesicle
why: Medorrhinum is the gonorrhoeal nosode; Psorinum is from the itch vesicle, Bacillinum from tubercular lung and Pyrogenium from decomposed beef.

q: Psorinum is prepared from:
opts: the contents of the scabies (itch) vesicle
why: Psorinum is the nosode of the itch vesicle; Syphilinum comes from the chancre.

q: A patient who feels unusually well the day before an attack of illness, with marked chilliness and offensive discharges, needs:
why: Psorinum (Allen's Keynotes): feels unusually well the day before an attack.

q: Pyrogenium was originally prepared from:
why: Pyrogenium was made by Drysdale from lean beef left to decompose in the sun; it is used in septic fevers.

q: Thuja occidentalis is commonly called:
why: Thuja occidentalis is arbor vitae; savine is Sabina, marsh tea Ledum and yellow jasmine Gelsemium.

q: Glonoinum is the homoeopathic preparation of:
why: Glonoinum is nitroglycerine, proved by Hering; silver nitrate is Argentum nitricum.

q: A fixed pain under the inferior angle of the right scapula, with liver complaints and jaundice, calls for the organ remedy:
why: Chelidonium: constant pain under the lower inner angle of the right scapula is its keynote; it is a leading liver remedy.

q: The remedy Cantharis is prepared from:
why: Cantharis vesicatoria is the Spanish fly, a blister beetle; the whole dried insect is used.

q: Hahnemann's Calcarea carbonica is prepared from:
opts: native chalk dug from the earth
the outer dark layer of the oyster shell
the middle, snow-white layer of the oyster shell
why: Calcarea carbonica (Calcarea ostrearum) is the impure calcium carbonate of the middle snow-white layer of the oyster shell.

q: Hepar sulphuris calcareum is prepared by:
opts: triturating sulphur with sugar of milk
dissolving calcium sulphate in strong alcohol
heating equal parts of powdered oyster shell and flowers of sulphur in a sealed crucible
distilling freshly slaked lime with potassium bisulphate
why: Hahnemann made Hepar sulph by heating finely powdered oyster shell with an equal part of flowers of sulphur in a hermetically closed crucible.

q: Causticum (Hahnemann's 'tinctura acris sine kali') is prepared by:
opts: heating oyster shell with flowers of sulphur
distilling freshly slaked lime with a solution of potassium bisulphate
why: Causticum is the distillate obtained from freshly burnt, slaked lime and a solution of bisulphate of potash.

q: Psorinum is prepared from:
opts: the sero-purulent matter of a scabies vesicle
the blood of a typhoid patient
why: Psorinum is a nosode made from the contents of the scabies (itch) vesicle.

q: Which of the following is NOT a nosode?
why: Pepsinum comes from the healthy stomach of an animal, so it is a sarcode; the others come from disease products.

q: Lyssinum (Hydrophobinum) is prepared from:
opts: the saliva of a rabid dog
the blood of a rabid dog after death
the brain of a healthy sheep
why: Lyssinum is a nosode prepared from the saliva of a rabid dog.

q: Pyrogenium is classically prepared from:
opts: the venom of the honey bee
the contents of a scabies vesicle
the sputum of a tuberculous patient
why: Pyrogenium (artificial sepsin) is made from lean beef allowed to decompose in water.

q: Mercurius solubilis of Hahnemann is chemically:
opts: a black oxide of mercury (dimercurous ammonium nitrate)
why: Hahnemann's soluble mercury is the black precipitate; mercuric chloride is Merc. cor., calomel is Merc. dulcis and metallic mercury is Merc. vivus.

q: Graphites used in homoeopathy is:
why: Graphites is plumbago or black lead; vegetable charcoal is Carbo veg., flint is Silicea and animal charcoal is Carbo animalis.

q: When medicinal plants are collected, seeds and fruits should be gathered:
opts: after the plant has withered in winter
why: Each part is collected when it is most active; for seeds and fruits that is when they are fully ripe.

q: Which of these remedies is prepared from seeds?
why: Nux vomica is made from the seeds; Cinchona uses the bark, Hydrastis the rhizome and Hamamelis the bark and twigs.

q: The size number of a globule (for example No. 10 or No. 30) indicates:
opts: the weight in milligrams of 10 globules
the number of globules in one gram
the number of globules medicated by one drop
the length in millimetres of 10 globules placed in a row
why: Globule number is the length in mm of ten globules laid side by side, so a No. 10 globule is about 1 mm across.

q: In the 'new method' of the HPI, most mother tinctures are prepared to a drug strength of:
why: The HPI new method standardises mother tinctures at a drug strength of 1/10 (one part dry drug substance in ten).

q: Under the HPI new method, a mother tincture of drug strength 1/10 is regarded as equivalent to:
why: A drug strength of 1/10 is itself one part in ten, so the Ø stands for 1X and 2X is made from it with 1 part Ø to 9 parts vehicle.

q: Under Hahnemann's old method, Class I drugs (fresh plants rich in juice) give a mother tincture with a drug strength of:
why: For Class I the expressed juice is mixed with an equal part of alcohol, so the drug strength is 1/2.

q: When Hahnemann's 3C trituration is dissolved in water and alcohol, the first liquid potency obtained is the:
why: Dissolving the 3C in water and alcohol is itself a further 1:100 step, so the first liquid potency is the 4C (equivalent to 8X).

q: In Hahnemann's method of trituration, each 20-minute stage consists of:
opts: 6 minutes grinding, 4 minutes scraping, 6 minutes grinding and 4 minutes scraping
15 minutes grinding followed by 5 minutes scraping
20 minutes of continuous grinding without scraping
10 minutes grinding followed by 10 minutes scraping
why: Each hour of trituration has three 20-minute stages, and each stage alternates 6 minutes of rubbing with 4 minutes of scraping, twice.

q: For one centesimal trituration, the 99 grains of sugar of milk are:
opts: divided into three equal parts, one part added at each 20-minute stage
added all at once at the start
added only after the drug has been ground alone
why: The 99 grains are split into three portions of 33 grains, one for each of the three 20-minute stages.

q: For the LM potency (Organon §270), one grain of the 3C trituration is dissolved in 500 drops of a mixture of:
opts: one part alcohol and four parts water
four parts alcohol and one part water
why: §270 directs that the grain be dissolved in 500 drops of a mixture of one part alcohol to four parts distilled water.

q: The 1 : 50,000 ratio of each LM step arises because:
opts: one drop is added to 100 drops of alcohol, and one medicated globule carries about 1/500 of a drop
fifty succussions are given to a 1:1000 dilution
each step adds one drop to 500 drops and gives 100 succussions
one grain is diluted in 50,000 grains of lactose
why: A drop moistens about 500 globules, so one globule holds about 1/500 drop; dissolving it and adding 100 drops gives 1/100 × 1/500 = 1/50,000.

q: According to §270, the vial in which an LM potency is succussed should be filled to about:
why: Hahnemann specified a vial two-thirds full, leaving room for the liquid to be struck forcefully during the 100 succussions.

q: A 3C potency corresponds in degree of dilution to:
why: Each centesimal step equals two decimal steps (1:100 = 1:10 × 1:10), so 3C = 6X.

q: The letter 'D' before a potency number, as used in Germany and Europe, indicates the:
why: D (decimal) is the European equivalent of X; 6D is the same as 6X.

q: Potencies written as 0/1, 0/2 or Q1, Q2 belong to the:
why: LM potencies are written 0/1, 0/2 and so on, or Q1, Q2 (Q for quinquagintamillesimal).

q: A potency labelled '200K' has been prepared by:
why: The suffix K marks potencies made by Korsakov's single-vial method.

q: Before the HPI was published, Indian manufacturers mainly followed:
opts: the American (HPUS) and German homoeopathic pharmacopoeias
the Indian Pharmacopoeia of allopathic drugs
why: Until the HPI appeared, Indian firms worked to the Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia of the United States and the German pharmacopoeia.

q: The standards of the HPI become legally binding because the Drugs and Cosmetics Act names the HPI in its:
why: The Second Schedule of the Act lists the standards drugs must meet; for homoeopathic medicines it names the HPI (and, failing that, other official homoeopathic pharmacopoeias).

q: In the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, 'homoeopathic medicines' are defined in Rule:
why: Rule 2(dd) defines homoeopathic medicines; Rule 30AA deals with import and Rule 67A with sale.

q: The manner of labelling homoeopathic medicines is laid down specifically in Rule:
why: Rule 106-A governs the labelling of homoeopathic medicines; Rules 96 and 97 deal with labelling of other drugs and Rule 65 with conditions of retail licences.

q: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, the label of a homoeopathic medicine must bear the words:
why: Rule 106-A requires the words 'Homoeopathic Medicine' on the label, along with the name, potency and other details.

q: A licence to sell homoeopathic medicines by wholesale is granted in Form:
why: Form 20-C is the retail licence and Form 20-D the wholesale licence for homoeopathic medicines; 25-C is the manufacturing licence.

q: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, a drug sold under the name of another drug, or falsely claiming to be made by a certain manufacturer, is termed:
why: Section 17-B defines spurious drugs (imitations and false claims of identity or maker); 17 covers misbranding and 17-A adulteration.

q: On a prescription, the 'subscription' gives:
opts: the patient's name, age and address
directions to the patient on how to take it
directions to the pharmacist on how to prepare or dispense the medicine
the name and potency of the medicine
why: The subscription instructs the dispenser; directions to the patient form the signatura.

q: The abbreviation 'stat.' on a prescription means:
why: Stat. is from the Latin statim, at once.

q: The abbreviation 'gtt.' on a prescription stands for:
why: Gtt. is short for guttae, drops.

q: The abbreviation 'q.s.' on a prescription means:
why: Q.s. is quantum sufficit, as much as is needed; 'as much as desired' is ad lib.

q: The abbreviation 'p.c.' on a prescription means:
why: P.c. is post cibum, after food.

q: The symbol 'Rx' at the head of a prescription comes from the Latin 'recipe', meaning:
why: Rx abbreviates recipe, 'take', the instruction to the dispenser to take the listed ingredients.

q: In the 6th edition of the Organon, §248 advises that the medicinal solution be:
opts: succussed a few times before each dose, so that each dose is slightly altered in potency
kept unshaken so that every dose has exactly the same potency
diluted 1:100 in fresh alcohol before each dose
why: §248 directs that the bottle be given several succussions before each dose, so repeated doses are not identical and are better tolerated.

q: In homoeopathic posology, the 'minimum dose' means:
opts: the lowest potency available in the pharmacy
a single drop of the mother tincture
the dose that just produces drug symptoms in the patient
the smallest quantity of the right remedy that is enough to bring about a gentle cure
why: The minimum dose is the smallest amount that still acts curatively, so that the medicinal aggravation is slight.

q: A preparation of a mother tincture in glycerin, used for external application, is called a:
why: A glycerole is a drug in glycerin; a liniment is an oily rubbing preparation, a cerate is wax-based and a collyrium is an eye lotion.

q: Tablets used in homoeopathy are made of:
why: Homoeopathic tablets are pressed from lactose; globules and pilules are made of cane sugar.

q: After soaking in the potency, medicated globules should be dried:
opts: in the shade, away from sunlight and strong heat
why: Heat and sunlight can damage the medicine, so medicated globules are dried in shade at room temperature.

q: Plants for homoeopathic drugs should preferably be collected:
opts: from their natural (wild) habitat, in dry and clear weather
at any time and place, as habitat does not matter
from cultivated gardens just after rain
in wet weather when the plant is full of sap
why: Wild plants from their natural habitat, gathered in dry weather, give the most typical and stable drug.

q: The word 'rubric' comes from the Latin for:
opts: red, because old books printed headings in red ink
why: Rubrica means red; headings were once printed in red, so a repertory heading is a rubric.

q: The word 'repertory' comes from the Latin 'repertorium', meaning:
opts: a storehouse, a place where things can be found
why: A repertorium is a storehouse or inventory, an index from which symptoms and remedies can be retrieved.

q: Hahnemann's first index of symptoms appeared as Part 2 of:
opts: the first edition of the Organon
why: The second part of the Fragmenta (1805) was an index of symptoms, the forerunner of the repertory.

q: Kent's Repertory contains how many chapters?
why: Kent's Repertory runs in 37 chapters, from Mind to Generalities.

q: Gentry's Concordance Repertory was published in:
why: W. D. Gentry's Concordance Repertory of the More Characteristic Symptoms appeared in six volumes (1890–92).

q: Within a rubric of Kent's Repertory, the sub-rubrics are arranged in the order:
opts: character, location, extension, conditions, time, side
side, time, conditions (modalities), extension, location, character
location, sensation, modality, concomitant, time, side
time, side, location, extension, character, conditions
why: Kent's fixed plan: sides first, then time, then modalities, then extension, then location and finally the character of the sensation.

q: In Kent's Repertory, the time sub-rubrics are listed in the order:
opts: morning, forenoon, noon, afternoon, evening, night, midnight
evening, night, midnight, morning, forenoon, noon, afternoon
night, midnight, morning, forenoon, noon, afternoon, evening
why: Kent lists time through the day starting from morning and ending with night and midnight (and after midnight).

q: In Kent's Repertory, dreams are found in the chapter:
why: Kent has no separate Dreams chapter; dreams are a rubric under Sleep.

q: Which of the following is NOT a separate chapter in Kent's Repertory?
why: Vision, Hearing and Expectoration are chapters; menstrual rubrics are found under Genitalia, Female.

q: In Kent's Repertory, palpitation of the heart is looked up in the chapter:
why: Kent has no Heart chapter; palpitation and heart symptoms sit in Chest.

q: In Kent's Repertory, symptoms of the nails are found in the chapter:
why: Nails are listed as part of the extremities, for example 'Extremities, Nails, brittle'.

q: In Kent's Repertory, nausea and vomiting are looked up in the chapter:
why: Nausea, vomiting, eructations and appetite rubrics are in Stomach.

q: In Kent's Repertory, the rubric for constipation is in the chapter:
why: Constipation and diarrhoea are rubrics of Rectum; Stool describes the character of the stool itself.

q: In Kent's Repertory, yawning is found in the chapter:
why: Kent places yawning under Sleep, alongside sleepiness and sleeplessness.

q: In Kent's Repertory, profuse sweat of the scalp (as in Calcarea carbonica) is looked up under:
why: The Perspiration chapter deals with sweat in general; sweat of one part, the scalp, is under Head.

q: In Kent's Repertory, difficult dentition in children is found in the chapter:
why: The rubric 'Dentition, difficult' is in Teeth.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven sections of Boenninghausen's Therapeutic Pocket Book?
why: TPB's sections are mind, parts of the body, sensations and complaints, sleep and dreams, fever, aggravations and ameliorations, and relationship; it has no disease section.

q: In Boenninghausen's seven-point scheme (Quis, Quid, Ubi, Quibus auxiliis, Cur, Quomodo, Quando), 'Quibus auxiliis' refers to:
why: Quibus auxiliis ('with what help') means the concomitants; Cur is the cause, Quando the time and Ubi the seat.

q: Phatak's Concise Repertory of Homoeopathic Medicines was built mainly on:
why: S. R. Phatak based his alphabetical repertory chiefly on C. M. Boger's Synoptic Key, enlarging it from other sources.

q: Boger's 'Boenninghausen's Characteristics and Repertory' (BBCR) was first published in:
why: BBCR appeared in 1905; the TPB was 1846, Kent's Repertory 1897 and Boger's Synoptic Key 1915.

q: The name of the software RADAR stands for:
opts: Rapid Aid to Drug Aimed Research
Rapid Analysis of Disease And Remedy
why: RADAR, from Archibel in Belgium, is short for Rapid Aid to Drug Aimed Research.

q: The homoeopathic software 'Hompath' was developed in India by:
why: Hompath is Dr Jawahar Shah's software; Schroyens edited Synthesis, Warkentin created MacRepertory and van Zandvoort the Complete Repertory.

q: MacRepertory, which uses the Complete Repertory, was created by:
why: MacRepertory is David Warkentin's software; van Zandvoort compiled the Complete Repertory used in it.

q: The Synthesis repertory is essentially:
opts: a translation of Boenninghausen's Therapeutic Pocket Book
a repertory of general symptoms only, in three volumes
a card repertory for mechanical elimination
an enlarged and corrected Kent's Repertory, with additions from many sources and author references
why: Synthesis builds on Kent's 6th edition with corrections, additions and source references; the three-volume generals-only work is Barthel and Klunker's Synthetic Repertory.

q: Barthel and Klunker's Synthetic Repertory is printed in:
opts: three languages: English, German and French
why: The Synthetic Repertory is trilingual, giving each rubric in English, German and French.

q: Repertories such as Gentry's and Knerr's are called 'Puritan' because they:
opts: keep the provers' own words without generalising them
why: Puritan repertories keep the original language of the provings rather than turning it into generalised rubrics.

q: Repertories such as Kent's, the TPB and BBCR, in which symptoms are reshaped to fit a fixed plan, belong to the:
why: These repertories follow a logical plan built on a philosophy, unlike the Puritan works that keep the provers' words.

q: A major limitation of card repertories is that they:
opts: need a computer to read the cards
ignore remedy grades, and one small card can wrongly exclude the true remedy
cannot be used for more than two rubrics
why: Holes show only presence or absence, so grading is lost, and any card lacking the remedy eliminates it.

q: In Kent's Repertory, a remedy printed in italics carries a value of:
why: Kent has three grades: bold type 3, italics 2 and plain roman 1.

q: The patient's statement 'I am always chilly' is classed as a:
why: It describes the whole person's reaction to temperature, so it is a physical general.

q: Headache in a patient suffering from a headache is an example of a:
why: A symptom found in nearly every case of that complaint does not help to individualise, so it is a common symptom.

q: Kent regarded menstrual symptoms as:
why: Kent held that menstrual state expresses the woman as a whole, so he ranked menstrual symptoms as generals.

q: A concomitant symptom is best defined as:
opts: a symptom left over from a past illness
a symptom occurring along with the chief complaint without an obvious pathological link to it
the factor that makes the complaint better or worse
why: A concomitant accompanies the chief complaint in time but is not explained by its pathology; the modifying factor is a modality.

q: Burning pains relieved by heat, or a dry mouth without thirst, are examples of:
why: They contradict what is expected, which makes them peculiar symptoms of high value (Organon §153).

q: After repertorisation, Remedy A covers all five chosen rubrics with 11 marks, while Remedy B has 13 marks but is absent from the most important rubric. Generally the physician should:
opts: always choose Remedy B because it has the higher total
choose whichever remedy has more bold-type entries
reject both and repeat the case taking
prefer Remedy A, and confirm it from the materia medica
why: Coverage of the key rubrics outweighs a bare marks total, and the final choice is always checked against the materia medica.

q: The rubric 'Mind, Censorious' means:
why: A censorious patient criticises and finds fault with others.

q: The rubric 'Mind, Fastidious' means:
opts: excessively particular about neatness and details
why: Fastidious patients, such as Arsenicum, insist on order and exactness in small things.

q: The rubric 'Mind, Loquacity' means:
why: Loquacity is talkativeness, as in Lachesis.

q: The rubric 'Mind, Ennui' means:
why: Ennui is boredom or tedium.

q: The rubric 'Mind, Mania-a-potu' refers to:
why: Mania-a-potu is mania from drink, that is, alcoholic delirium.

q: A patient says she always feels guilty, as if she had committed some crime. The most suitable Kent rubric is:
opts: Mind, Delusions, persecuted, that he is
Mind, Anxiety, conscience, of (as if guilty of a crime)
why: Kent's rubric 'Anxiety of conscience, as if guilty of a crime' converts this expression exactly.

q: A patient says, 'Nobody cares for me; I am all alone in this world.' The best rubric is:
why: The feeling of being isolated and uncared for is rubric-converted to 'Forsaken feeling'.

q: In repertory language, 'opisthotonos' means:
opts: bending of the body to one side
spasmodic arching of the body backwards
spasmodic bending of the body forwards
why: Opisthotonos is backward arching; forward bending is emprosthotonos and sideways bending pleurothotonos.

q: The term 'strangury' in a rubric means:
opts: slow, painful passing of urine drop by drop with straining
passing large amounts of urine at night
why: Strangury is painful, drop-by-drop urination with tenesmus, as in Cantharis.

q: A 'lienteric' stool is one that:
why: Lientery is the passing of food undigested in the stool.

q: The first bone in the body to begin ossification is the:
why: The clavicle begins to ossify in membrane in the 5th–6th week of intrauterine life.

q: A fall on the outstretched hand causes tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox; the proximal fragment later undergoes avascular necrosis. The bone fractured is the:
why: Scaphoid fracture is the commonest carpal fracture; its blood enters distally, so the proximal fragment may necrose.

q: Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus endangers the:
why: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels.

q: Winging of the scapula on pushing against a wall is due to injury of the:
why: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) supplies serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the chest wall.

q: A baby delivered with the arm pulled upward develops claw hand with Horner's syndrome on that side. The lesion is in the:
opts: lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1)
upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6)
why: This is Klumpke's palsy; T1 involvement interrupts the sympathetic outflow to the head, giving Horner's syndrome.

q: The joint between a tooth and its socket is a:
why: A gomphosis is a peg-and-socket fibrous joint, held by the periodontal ligament.

q: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is a synovial joint of the:
why: The oval radial surface and the convex carpal surface form an ellipsoid joint allowing flexion, extension, abduction and adduction.

q: The commonest site of a stroke causing contralateral hemiplegia, because motor fibres are packed tightly there, is the:
opts: posterior limb of the internal capsule
why: Corticospinal fibres crowd through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, so a small lesion there causes dense contralateral hemiplegia.

q: Parkinsonism results mainly from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the:
why: Degeneration of the nigrostriatal dopamine pathway from the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease.

q: A lesion of the primary visual cortex of one occipital lobe typically produces:
opts: total blindness of the eye on the same side
contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
why: The visual cortex receives the opposite half-field of both eyes; the macula is often spared owing to dual blood supply. Bitemporal loss is from the optic chiasma.

q: The ankle jerk tests the spinal segments:
why: The Achilles reflex is S1–S2; the knee jerk is L3–L4 and the biceps jerk C5–C6.

q: Which of the following findings favours a lower motor neuron lesion?
why: LMN lesions give flaccid weakness, wasting, fasciculations and lost reflexes; the other three are UMN signs.

q: In hemisection of the spinal cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome), pain and temperature sensation are lost:
opts: on both sides below the lesion
on the opposite side, beginning a segment or two below the lesion
on the same side below the lesion
only at the level of the lesion on the opposite side
why: Spinothalamic fibres cross within one or two segments, so pain and temperature are lost contralaterally; dorsal-column sensation and motor power are lost on the same side.

q: After a stroke, a patient cannot smile on one side but can still wrinkle the forehead on both sides. The forehead is spared because:
opts: the lesion is in the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
the part of the facial nucleus supplying the upper face receives cortical fibres from both hemispheres
the forehead muscles have no motor supply
the forehead muscles are supplied by the trigeminal nerve
why: In UMN facial palsy only the lower face is weak; a lesion of the nerve itself (LMN, as in Bell's palsy) paralyses the whole half of the face.

q: Cerebrospinal fluid is mainly produced by the:
why: The choroid plexuses secrete CSF; arachnoid granulations absorb it into the venous sinuses.

q: The second heart sound is produced by closure of the:
why: S2 marks the end of ventricular systole when the semilunar valves close.

q: On the ECG, the T wave represents:
opts: conduction delay in the AV node
why: P is atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation and T ventricular repolarisation.

q: On a standard ECG recorded at 25 mm/s, the R–R interval is 4 large squares. The heart rate is about:
why: Each large square is 0.2 s; heart rate = 300 ÷ number of large squares = 300 ÷ 4 = 75/min.

q: Tall, peaked T waves on the ECG are characteristic of:
why: Raised potassium speeds repolarisation and produces tall tented T waves; hypokalaemia gives flat T waves and U waves.

q: Starling's law of the heart states that:
opts: stroke volume falls as venous return rises
the force of ventricular contraction increases with the end-diastolic fibre length (preload)
heart rate rises whenever blood pressure falls
cardiac contraction is independent of ventricular filling
why: Within limits, greater filling stretches the fibres and produces a stronger contraction, matching output to venous return.

q: Renin is secreted by the:
opts: cells of the proximal convoluted tubule
juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole
why: The juxtaglomerular (granular) cells secrete renin; the macula densa senses tubular NaCl and signals them.

q: The main lung volumes that add up to the vital capacity are:
opts: tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume only
inspiratory reserve volume + tidal volume + expiratory reserve volume
why: Vital capacity is the maximum air that can be expired after a maximal inspiration: IRV + TV + ERV (about 4.5–4.8 L).

q: The functional residual capacity is the sum of:
why: FRC is the air left in the lungs at the end of a quiet expiration: ERV + RV (about 2.3–2.5 L).

q: The main stimulus to the central chemoreceptors of the medulla is:
opts: a rise in H⁺ concentration in the CSF produced by CO₂
a fall in arterial blood pressure
why: CO₂ crosses into the CSF and forms H⁺, which drives the central chemoreceptors; hypoxia acts on the peripheral (carotid and aortic) chemoreceptors.

q: Most of the carbon dioxide in blood is carried as:
why: About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate formed by carbonic anhydrase in red cells.

q: The normal glomerular filtration rate in an adult is about:
why: GFR is about 125 mL/min (180 L/day); 650 mL/min is about the renal plasma flow and 1.2 L/min the renal blood flow.

q: The clearance of para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is used to measure:
why: PAH is filtered and secreted so completely that its clearance approximates renal plasma flow.

q: If GFR is 125 mL/min and renal plasma flow is 625 mL/min, the filtration fraction is:
why: Filtration fraction = GFR ÷ RPF = 125 ÷ 625 = 0.2, that is 20%.

q: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) begins the digestion of:
why: Ptyalin splits starch into maltose and dextrins in the mouth.

q: Pancreatic trypsinogen is activated in the duodenum by:
why: Enterokinase from the duodenal mucosa converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic proenzymes.

q: After digestion, long-chain fatty acids leave the intestinal cells mainly as:
opts: fatty acids bound to albumin in the hepatic artery
free fatty acids entering the portal vein
why: Long-chain fats are re-esterified and packed into chylomicrons, which enter the lymph via lacteals; short-chain fatty acids go to the portal blood.

q: In the liver, bilirubin is made water-soluble by conjugation with:
why: UDP-glucuronyl transferase conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid; albumin only carries unconjugated bilirubin in plasma.

q: Antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin are synthesised in the:
opts: supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus
why: They are made in hypothalamic neurons, carried down their axons and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary.

q: Low serum T4 with a high TSH indicates:
why: A failing thyroid removes negative feedback, so the pituitary raises TSH; in pituitary failure both T4 and TSH are low.

q: Long-term corticosteroid therapy must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly because:
opts: the kidneys can no longer excrete potassium
the steroids have permanently destroyed the pituitary
negative feedback has suppressed CRH and ACTH, and the adrenal cortex has atrophied
the liver has stopped making cortisol-binding globulin
why: Exogenous steroid suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; abrupt withdrawal can cause acute adrenal insufficiency.

q: Total body water in an average adult man is about what share of body weight?
why: About 60% of body weight is water: two-thirds intracellular (40%) and one-third extracellular (20%).

q: Generalised oedema in nephrotic syndrome is mainly due to:
opts: loss of red cells into the tissues
a fall in capillary hydrostatic pressure
a fall in plasma colloid osmotic pressure
why: Heavy proteinuria lowers plasma albumin, so oncotic pressure falls and fluid leaves the capillaries.

q: At a normal blood pH of 7.4, the ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid is:
why: By the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH 7.4 = 6.1 + log 20, so HCO₃⁻ : H₂CO₃ is 20 : 1.

q: Arterial blood shows pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 30 mEq/L. This is:
opts: respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation
why: Low pH with raised PaCO₂ is respiratory acidosis; the raised bicarbonate is renal compensation, incomplete because the pH is still low.

q: Diabetic ketoacidosis typically produces:
opts: high anion gap metabolic acidosis with deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing
why: Ketoacids add unmeasured anions, widening the anion gap; the lungs compensate by blowing off CO₂.

q: The desirable level of total serum cholesterol in adults is:
why: Below 200 mg/dL is desirable, 200–239 borderline high and 240 or more high.

q: The most specific serum marker of myocardial injury is:
why: Troponins are specific to heart muscle and stay raised for days; CK-MB, AST and LDH are less specific.

q: In the WHO oral glucose tolerance test, an adult is given:
why: The standard OGTT uses 75 g of anhydrous glucose; a 2-hour value of 200 mg/dL or more indicates diabetes.

q: After about 24 hours of fasting, blood glucose is maintained mainly by:
opts: absorption of glucose from the gut
release of free glucose from muscle glycogen
why: Liver glycogen is largely used up within about a day; muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot release free glucose.

q: A competitive inhibitor of an enzyme:
opts: lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged
raises Vmax but leaves Km unchanged
raises the apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged
why: The inhibitor competes for the active site, so more substrate is needed for half-maximal velocity, but enough substrate still reaches the same Vmax.

q: The earliest change of reversible cell injury seen on light microscopy is:
why: Failure of membrane ion pumps lets water enter the cell, producing cellular swelling, the first and reversible change; nuclear changes indicate irreversible injury.

q: An infarct in which of the following organs typically undergoes liquefactive necrosis?
why: Ischaemic death of CNS tissue produces liquefactive necrosis; infarcts of other solid organs show coagulative necrosis.

q: Fibrinoid necrosis of arteriolar walls is characteristic of:
why: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in immune-mediated vasculitis and in malignant hypertension, where fibrin leaks into damaged arteriolar walls.

q: The principal mediator of the immediate, transient increase in vascular permeability in acute inflammation is:
why: Histamine released from mast cells causes arteriolar dilatation and endothelial contraction in venules within seconds, giving the immediate transient response.

q: In a healing wound, the collagen laid down first in granulation tissue, later replaced by type I collagen, is:
why: Early granulation tissue contains mainly type III collagen, which is gradually replaced by the stronger type I collagen during remodelling.

q: Excessive scar tissue that grows beyond the margins of the original wound and does not regress is called a:
why: A keloid extends beyond the wound boundary and seldom regresses; a hypertrophic scar stays within the wound margins.

q: A rubbery intravascular clot with a dark-red dependent 'currant-jelly' part and a yellow 'chicken-fat' upper part, not attached to the vessel wall, is a:
why: Post-mortem clots form after death as red cells settle, giving currant-jelly and chicken-fat layers; they lack lines of Zahn and wall attachment.

q: A deep-vein thrombus that reaches the systemic arterial circulation through a patent foramen ovale is called:
why: Paradoxical (crossed) embolism occurs when a venous embolus passes through an interatrial or interventricular defect into the systemic arteries.

q: The histological grading of a malignant tumour is based mainly on its:
opts: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity
why: Grade reflects how closely tumour cells resemble normal cells (differentiation) and mitotic count; size, nodes and metastases determine the stage.

q: The single feature that most reliably marks a tumour as malignant is:
why: Metastasis unequivocally marks a tumour as malignant; benign tumours never metastasise.

q: Spread by seeding of body cavities, producing multiple peritoneal deposits, is most characteristic of carcinoma of the:
why: Transcoelomic seeding of the peritoneal cavity is classically seen with ovarian carcinoma.

q: Mallory-Denk bodies (Mallory hyaline) in hepatocytes are most characteristic of:
why: Mallory hyaline consists of damaged intermediate (keratin) filaments and is a hallmark of alcoholic hepatitis; apoptotic Councilman bodies occur in viral hepatitis.

q: The test that distinguishes Staphylococcus aureus from other staphylococci is the:
why: S. aureus is coagulase positive; catalase is positive for all staphylococci, and bile solubility identifies pneumococci.

q: The medium routinely used to culture Mycobacterium tuberculosis is:
opts: Thiosulphate citrate bile salt sucrose agar
why: Egg-based Lowenstein-Jensen medium is the standard solid medium for M. tuberculosis; colonies appear in 2 to 8 weeks.

q: In chronic typhoid carriers the bacilli most often persist in the:
why: Chronic carriers harbour Salmonella Typhi in the gall bladder (often with gallstones) and excrete it in faeces.

q: Culture of faeces in typhoid fever is most often positive during the:
why: Blood culture is positive in the first week, Widal from the second, and stool culture mainly in the third and fourth weeks ('BASU' sequence).

q: In hepatitis B infection, the serum marker indicating active viral replication and high infectivity is:
why: HBeAg correlates with high levels of HBV DNA and infectivity; seroconversion to anti-HBe indicates reduced replication.

q: A person who has been vaccinated against hepatitis B but never infected will show in serum:
why: The vaccine contains only HBsAg, so it induces anti-HBs alone; anti-HBc appears only after natural infection.

q: Hepatitis D virus can cause infection only in the presence of:
why: HDV is a defective RNA virus that needs HBsAg for its envelope, so it occurs only as co-infection or superinfection with HBV.

q: Severe dengue (dengue haemorrhagic fever) is more likely in a second infection with a different serotype because of:
why: Non-neutralising antibodies from the first infection enhance entry of the new serotype into monocytes, increasing viral load and plasma leakage.

q: Enlarged red cells containing Schuffner's dots on a peripheral smear are seen in infection with:
why: P. vivax (and P. ovale) infect young red cells, which enlarge and show Schuffner's dots; P. falciparum shows Maurer's clefts.

q: The stage of the malaria parasite injected into man by the female Anopheles mosquito is the:
why: Sporozoites from the mosquito's salivary glands enter the blood and go to the liver to begin exo-erythrocytic schizogony.

q: Skin scrapings are examined for fungal hyphae in suspected dermatophytosis after treatment with:
why: KOH (10 to 20%) digests keratin so that fungal hyphae can be seen in direct mounts of skin, hair and nail.

q: The mature cyst of Entamoeba histolytica contains:
why: The mature infective cyst of E. histolytica is quadrinucleate; the cyst of the non-pathogenic E. coli has up to eight nuclei.

q: The normal platelet count in adults is about:
why: Normal platelets are 150,000 to 450,000/uL; 4,000 to 11,000 is the WBC range and 4.5 to 5.5 million the RBC count.

q: Macrocytic anaemia is defined by a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) above:
why: Normal MCV is about 80 to 100 fL; values above 100 fL indicate macrocytosis, as in vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

q: A raised reticulocyte count is most typical of:
why: Reticulocytosis reflects increased marrow output in response to red cell destruction or blood loss; it is low in marrow failure and deficiency states.

q: The total leucocyte count in uncomplicated typhoid fever typically shows:
why: Typhoid characteristically causes leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis and absent eosinophils; leucocytosis suggests a complication such as perforation.

q: Prolonged bleeding time with a low platelet count but normal PT and aPTT in an otherwise well child after a viral illness suggests:
why: Isolated thrombocytopenia prolongs bleeding time while coagulation tests stay normal; haemophilia prolongs aPTT, and vitamin K deficiency and DIC prolong PT.

q: In liver function tests, an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2 suggests:
why: Alcohol causes pyridoxal phosphate deficiency and mitochondrial damage, so AST rises more than ALT; viral hepatitis usually shows ALT above AST.

q: Low serum albumin with a prolonged prothrombin time not corrected by vitamin K indicates:
opts: Impaired synthetic function of the liver
why: Albumin and clotting factors are made by hepatocytes; failure of both, unresponsive to vitamin K, indicates loss of liver cell mass, as in cirrhosis.

q: A blood urea nitrogen (BUN) to creatinine ratio above 20:1 most suggests:
why: In prerenal states urea is reabsorbed avidly along with water, raising BUN out of proportion to creatinine; in intrinsic renal damage the ratio is usually below 15.

q: Proteinuria in the nephrotic range in an adult is a urinary protein excretion of more than:
why: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia; normal excretion is below 150 mg/day.

q: White blood cell casts in urine are characteristic of:
why: WBC casts form in the tubules and so localise inflammation to the kidney, as in pyelonephritis; cystitis gives pus cells without casts.

q: Rothera's test on urine detects:
why: Rothera's nitroprusside test gives a purple ring with acetoacetate and acetone; Benedict's detects glucose and Hay's test bile salts.

q: The normal serum creatinine in an adult is about:
why: Normal serum creatinine is about 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL; 20 to 40 mg/dL is the usual range for blood urea.

q: On a chest X-ray, a homogeneous lobar opacity containing air bronchograms most suggests:
opts: Collapse due to an obstructing tumour
why: Air bronchograms show air-filled bronchi within alveoli filled with exudate, the sign of consolidation; effusion and obstructive collapse do not show them.

q: Cavitation with fibrosis in the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobe on a chest X-ray is typical of:
why: Post-primary TB favours the well-oxygenated upper lobes and cavitates; primary TB gives a Ghon focus with hilar lymphadenopathy.

q: A sharp visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it on a chest X-ray indicates:
why: Air in the pleural space separates the visceral pleura from the chest wall, leaving a hyperlucent area without lung markings.

q: On a PA chest X-ray, cardiomegaly is suggested by a cardiothoracic ratio greater than:
why: A cardiothoracic ratio above 50% on a standard PA film suggests cardiac enlargement; AP films exaggerate heart size.

q: Kerley B lines on a chest X-ray indicate:
why: Kerley B lines are short horizontal lines at the lung bases from fluid-thickened interlobular septa, as in left ventricular failure.

q: On abdominal ultrasonography, fatty liver typically appears as a liver with:
opts: A shrunken nodular outline with ascites
why: Fat in hepatocytes increases reflectivity, so the liver looks brighter than the kidney cortex; a small nodular liver with ascites suggests cirrhosis.

q: The serological marker most specific for rheumatoid arthritis is:
why: Anti-CCP has a specificity of about 95% for RA; rheumatoid factor is also found in other diseases and in healthy elderly people.

q: Which of the following is a specific treponemal test for syphilis?
why: TPHA detects antibodies against Treponema pallidum antigens; VDRL, RPR and Kahn are non-treponemal tests using cardiolipin.

q: In the Weil-Felix test, agglutination of the Proteus OX-K strain alone suggests:
why: Orientia tsutsugamushi gives OX-K agglutination; epidemic and endemic typhus react with OX-19, and Q fever is Weil-Felix negative.

q: A very high blood pressure is termed a hypertensive emergency, rather than urgency, when there is:
opts: A diastolic BP above 120 mmHg without symptoms
Failure to respond to three antihypertensive drugs
why: A hypertensive emergency is severe BP elevation with acute organ damage (encephalopathy, LVF, dissection, AKI); without it the situation is urgency.

q: Hypertension with hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and suppressed plasma renin, without Cushingoid features, most suggests:
why: Autonomous aldosterone excess causes sodium retention, potassium loss and alkalosis, with renin suppressed; renal artery stenosis raises renin.

q: Chest pain at rest, often in the early morning, with transient ST-segment elevation that settles with nitrates and normal troponin, is typical of:
why: Variant angina results from coronary artery spasm, giving transient ST elevation at rest; pericarditis gives widespread, persistent concave ST elevation.

q: In a patient with ischaemic chest pain at rest and ST depression, the finding that distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina is:
why: Both present alike; NSTEMI is diagnosed when troponin rises, indicating myocardial necrosis, while unstable angina has normal troponin.

q: Which of these is a feature of LIFE-THREATENING acute asthma?
why: A silent chest, cyanosis, SpO2 below 92%, PEF below 33% and exhaustion mark life-threatening asthma; HR 110 and RR 25 mark acute severe asthma.

q: A thin, breathless COPD patient with pursed-lip breathing, a hyperinflated chest and near-normal blood gases until late is described as a:
why: Emphysema-dominant patients hyperventilate to keep oxygenation ('pink puffers'); bronchitis-dominant patients are hypoxic, cyanosed and oedematous ('blue bloaters').

q: Pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm and leg without aphasia, visual field loss or sensory deficit in a long-standing hypertensive suggests:
why: Lacunar infarcts from hypertensive small-vessel disease in the internal capsule cause pure motor or pure sensory strokes without cortical signs.

q: Contralateral hemiparesis affecting the face and arm more than the leg, with aphasia when the dominant side is involved, indicates occlusion of the:
why: The MCA supplies the lateral cortex representing face and arm and the speech areas; ACA occlusion affects the leg more, and PCA occlusion causes hemianopia.

q: The antiepileptic drug most strongly associated with neural tube defects when used in pregnancy is:
why: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk, including spina bifida, and is avoided in women of childbearing potential where possible.

q: Multiple, recurrent peptic ulcers including in the jejunum, with diarrhoea and very high gastric acid output, suggest a:
why: Gastrin from a pancreatic or duodenal gastrinoma drives massive acid secretion, causing refractory ulcers at unusual sites and diarrhoea.

q: Barrett's oesophagus, a complication of long-standing GERD, is:
opts: Squamous metaplasia of the lower oesophagus with risk of squamous carcinoma
Failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter
Columnar (intestinal) metaplasia of the lower oesophagus with risk of adenocarcinoma
A mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction after vomiting
why: Chronic acid reflux replaces squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium, which predisposes to oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
