q: Under the Rome IV criteria, IBS requires recurrent abdominal pain on average at least:
opts: 3 days per month in the last 3 months
1 day per week in the last 3 months
Once a month for a year
why: Rome IV: pain at least 1 day a week for 3 months, with symptom onset at least 6 months before, linked to defecation or change in stool frequency or form; '3 days per month' was Rome III.

q: A first-line oral antiviral for chronic hepatitis B is:
why: Tenofovir and entecavir are potent nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high barrier to resistance used for chronic HBV.

q: Primary prophylaxis against bleeding from large oesophageal varices in cirrhosis can be given with a non-selective beta-blocker such as:
why: Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol, nadolol, carvedilol) lower portal pressure by reducing cardiac output and splanchnic flow; cardioselective atenolol does not.

q: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in a cirrhotic with ascites is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid:
opts: Neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or more
why: An ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250/mm3 is diagnostic of SBP; a SAAG above 1.1 only indicates portal hypertension.

q: Fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot's triad) indicate:
why: Charcot's triad reflects infection of an obstructed common bile duct; adding confusion and hypotension gives Reynolds' pentad.

q: Acute cholecystitis is most commonly caused by:
opts: Impaction of a gallstone in the cystic duct
Salmonella infection of the gall bladder
why: About 90% of acute cholecystitis is calculous, due to a stone obstructing the cystic duct; acalculous disease occurs in the critically ill.

q: Impaired glucose tolerance is defined by a 2-hour plasma glucose, after a 75 g oral glucose load, of:
why: A 2-hour value of 140 to 199 mg/dL is IGT, 200 or more is diabetes; 100 to 125 mg/dL fasting defines impaired fasting glucose.

q: Metformin is contraindicated when the eGFR falls below:
why: Because of the risk of lactic acidosis, metformin is stopped below an eGFR of 30, and the dose is reviewed or reduced between 30 and 45.

q: A hypothyroid woman with a firm, painless goitre and strongly positive anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies most likely has:
why: Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis, with anti-TPO antibodies, is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas.

q: A painful, tender thyroid after an upper respiratory infection, with fever, raised ESR, transient thyrotoxicosis and low radioiodine uptake, suggests:
why: Viral inflammation releases stored hormone, so thyrotoxicosis occurs with low uptake; Graves' and toxic nodules show high uptake and are painless.

q: Which of the following is used to treat an acute attack of gout?
why: NSAIDs such as indomethacin, colchicine or corticosteroids treat the acute attack; allopurinol, febuxostat and probenecid are urate-lowering drugs for long-term control.

q: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in a chronic alcoholic indicate deficiency of:
why: This is Wernicke's encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency; parenteral thiamine must be given before glucose.

q: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is caused by deficiency of:
why: B12 deficiency damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, causing loss of joint position and vibration sense with spastic weakness.

q: A chronic, itchy eczema of the antecubital and popliteal fossae in a young adult with a personal history of asthma and hay fever is most likely:
why: Atopic eczema affects the flexures in older children and adults and is associated with asthma and allergic rhinitis; psoriasis favours extensor surfaces.

q: Pitting of the nails with onycholysis is most characteristic of:
why: Nail pitting, onycholysis and 'oil-drop' discolouration occur in psoriasis; iron deficiency gives koilonychia.

q: Urticaria is termed chronic when wheals recur for more than:
why: Urticaria lasting more than 6 weeks is chronic; second-generation H1 antihistamines are the first-line drugs.

q: In measles, the rash typically appears on about the:
opts: 1st day of fever, on the trunk
2nd day of fever, on the palms and soles
4th day of fever, starting behind the ears and along the hairline
7th day of fever, on the abdomen
why: The maculopapular measles rash appears around day 4, starting behind the ears and at the hairline, then spreading downwards.

q: Fever, sore throat, a strawberry tongue, a fine 'sandpaper' rash with circumoral pallor and Pastia's lines suggest:
why: Scarlet fever, due to erythrogenic toxin of Group A streptococcus, gives this rash with accentuation in skin folds (Pastia's lines).

q: Fever with conjunctival suffusion, calf tenderness, jaundice and acute kidney injury after wading in flood water during the monsoon suggests:
why: Weil's disease is the icteric, haemorrhagic and renal form of leptospirosis; conjunctival suffusion and calf tenderness are typical.

q: Radical cure of Plasmodium vivax malaria under the Indian national programme requires, after G6PD consideration:
why: Primaquine (0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days) kills the liver hypnozoites that cause relapse; chloroquine treats only the blood stage.

q: Which of these is a WHO warning sign in dengue that calls for close monitoring or admission?
why: Warning signs include abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement and rising haematocrit with falling platelets.

q: The antiviral drug used for treating influenza, including H1N1, is:
why: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor used for influenza A and B, best within 48 hours of onset.

q: Angina with a sensation as if the heart were grasped by an iron hand, worse lying on the left side, calls for:
why: Constriction 'as if by an iron band or hand' around the heart and chest is the keynote of Cactus grandiflorus.

q: The mother tincture often used in homoeopathic practice for high blood pressure is:
why: Rauwolfia Q is used for hypertension; Syzygium is used for diabetes, Blatta for asthma and Berberis for renal colic.

q: Asthma or spasmodic cough with constant nausea not relieved by vomiting and a clean tongue calls for:
why: Persistent nausea with a clean tongue is the keynote of Ipecac; the chest seems full of phlegm that does not come up.

q: Bronchitis in an old person with coarse rattling of mucus but very little expectoration, drowsiness and a thick white-coated tongue calls for:
why: Ant tart has loud rattling with little expectoration, drowsiness and prostration, typical in the very young and the very old.

q: Right-sided facial (Bell's) palsy after exposure to dry cold wind, in a patient prone to paralysis of single parts, calls for:
why: Causticum is the leading remedy for local paralyses of single parts such as the face, vocal cords and bladder, especially after cold dry wind.

q: Epileptic convulsions that begin with cramps in the fingers and toes, thumbs clenched into the palms and a blue face, call for:
why: Cuprum has violent cramps and spasms beginning in the fingers and toes, with clenched thumbs and cyanosis.

q: A gastric ulcer that is round and 'punched out', with pain felt in a small spot, calls for:
why: Kali bich has deep, round, punched-out ulcers on mucous membranes and pains in small spots that can be covered with a fingertip.

q: Intense hyperacidity with sour eructations and sour vomiting, worse at night on lying down, with frontal headache, calls for:
why: Robinia is the classic remedy for hyperchlorhydria with intensely sour eructations and vomiting, worse at night lying down.

q: Irritable bowel with diarrhoea from anticipation before an event, craving for sweets that disagree, and flatulence with loud belching calls for:
why: Anticipatory anxiety, craving for sweets that aggravate, and loud explosive belching are keynotes of Argentum nitricum.

q: Jaundice with an enlarged, tender liver, clay-coloured stools and a tendency to gallstones, for which the mother tincture is often used, calls for:
why: Chionanthus is a liver remedy for jaundice, hepatic enlargement, clay-coloured stools and gallstone colic.

q: Diabetes following grief, with apathy, indifference, weakness and profuse, milky urine at night, calls for:
why: Phosphoric acid suits debility from grief with mental apathy and profuse, frequent, milky urine.

q: Hyperthyroidism with emaciation despite a ravenous appetite, anxiety when hungry, relief from eating and intolerance of heat, calls for:
why: Iodum patients lose flesh while eating well, feel better after eating and are warm-blooded; it is used for goitre and thyrotoxicosis.

q: Gout that begins in the feet and travels upward, with joints cold to touch yet relieved by cold applications, calls for:
why: Ledum has ascending rheumatic and gouty pains in small joints that are cold yet better from cold bathing.

q: Eczema with thick, leathery crusts under which thick white pus collects, with intolerable itching, calls for:
why: Mezereum has eruptions covered by thick, hard crusts with pus beneath, intensely itchy, especially on the scalp.

q: Urticaria with burning, itching blotches following the eating of shellfish calls for:
why: Urtica urens has burning, stinging urticaria and is noted for ailments from eating shellfish.

q: Chickenpox with intensely itching vesicles, restlessness and relief from warmth and motion calls for:
why: Rhus tox suits vesicular eruptions with intense itching and restlessness, better from warmth, as in chickenpox and herpes zoster.

q: Hahnemann recommended which remedy as a prophylactic in epidemics of smooth (Sydenham's) scarlet fever?
why: In 1801 Hahnemann described Belladonna as the prophylactic for the smooth, bright-red type of scarlet fever, an early use of the genus epidemicus idea.

q: A primigravida usually first perceives fetal movements (quickening) at about:
why: Quickening is felt at about 20 weeks in a primigravida and about 2 weeks earlier in a multigravida.

q: Under Anemia Mukt Bharat, a pregnant woman takes one IFA tablet (60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid) daily from the second trimester for at least:
why: Prophylactic IFA is given daily from the 4th month of pregnancy for a minimum of 180 days, and continued for 180 days post partum.

q: The drug of choice for the prevention and control of eclamptic convulsions is:
why: Magnesium sulphate (Pritchard or Zuspan regimen) is superior to diazepam and phenytoin for eclampsia.

q: While a woman is on magnesium sulphate, the first clinical sign of toxicity to watch for is:
why: Knee jerk disappears at serum levels around 10 mEq/L, before respiratory depression; so the reflex is checked before every repeat dose.

q: Which antihypertensive is contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios?
why: ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic; labetalol, methyldopa and nifedipine are the accepted antihypertensives in pregnancy.

q: A large (macrosomic) baby of a mother with gestational diabetes is especially prone, during vaginal delivery, to:
why: Fetal macrosomia, with disproportionately large shoulders, makes shoulder dystocia a classic intrapartum hazard in diabetic pregnancy.

q: The third stage of labour extends from:
opts: onset of true labour pains to full cervical dilatation
delivery of the baby to expulsion of the placenta and membranes
full cervical dilatation to delivery of the baby
expulsion of the placenta to one hour after delivery
why: The third stage is the placental stage; the hour after it is often called the fourth stage (observation).

q: In active management of the third stage of labour, the uterotonic of choice is:
opts: ergometrine 0.5 mg IV before delivery of the shoulder
misoprostol 1000 mcg rectally after the placenta
oxytocin 10 IU IM within one minute of birth
why: WHO and Indian guidelines recommend oxytocin 10 IU IM as the first-choice uterotonic for AMTSL.

q: At the onset of labour, the commonest position of a vertex presentation is:
why: Left occipito-anterior is the commonest position, followed by right occipito-posterior.

q: On the WHO partograph, the alert line represents a rate of cervical dilatation of:
why: The alert line starts in the active phase and slopes at 1 cm/hour; the action line is drawn 4 hours to its right.

q: Irregular, spasmodic false labour pains that fly about the abdomen, with a rigid os and great exhaustion, call for:
why: Caulophyllum is the classic remedy for spasmodic, ineffectual pains with rigidity of the os and weakness.

q: Constant nausea in pregnancy not relieved by vomiting, with a clean tongue, calls for:
why: Persistent nausea unrelieved by vomiting with a clean tongue is the keynote of Ipecac; Nux and Ant crud have coated tongues.

q: An unsensitised Rh-negative mother who delivers an Rh-positive baby should receive anti-D immunoglobulin:
opts: 300 mcg IM within 72 hours of delivery
300 mcg IM only before the next pregnancy
50 mcg IV within 7 days of delivery
only if the baby is jaundiced
why: A standard 300 mcg (1500 IU) dose IM within 72 hours neutralises fetal red cells entering the maternal circulation.

q: A 'chocolate cyst' of the ovary is characteristic of:
why: An endometrioma contains old altered blood that looks like chocolate.

q: The two commonest sexually transmitted organisms causing pelvic inflammatory disease are:
opts: Treponema pallidum and Herpes simplex virus
why: Chlamydia and gonococcus ascend from the cervix to the tubes; the others cause lower genital or ulcerative disease.

q: The commonest type of uterine fibroid by location is:
why: About 75% of fibroids are intramural; submucous are fewest but bleed most.

q: Red (carneous) degeneration of a fibroid most often occurs:
opts: during pregnancy, usually in the second trimester
in the first year after menarche
during lactation after the sixth month
why: Red degeneration is a haemorrhagic infarction typically seen in mid-pregnancy, causing acute pain and fever.

q: Long-standing PCOS with chronic anovulation increases the risk of:
why: Unopposed oestrogen without progesterone leads to endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma.

q: In visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) screening for cervical cancer, the cervix is painted with:
why: Abnormal epithelium turns acetowhite with 3–5% acetic acid; Lugol's iodine is used for VILI.

q: Carcinoma of the cervix is most strongly associated with infection by:
why: High-risk HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers.

q: The commonest germ-cell tumour of the ovary is the:
why: Benign cystic teratoma is the commonest germ-cell tumour and the commonest ovarian tumour in young women.

q: Meigs' syndrome is ascites and right-sided hydrothorax associated with:
opts: a granulosa cell tumour of the uterus
why: Classic Meigs' syndrome is a benign ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion that resolve after removal.

q: The pain of primary dysmenorrhoea is mainly due to excess endometrial production of:
why: PGF2α causes myometrial hypercontractility and ischaemia, which is why NSAIDs relieve it.

q: Dysmenorrhoea in which the pains are relieved as soon as the menstrual flow begins is a keynote of:
why: Lachesis is better once the discharge is established; in Cimicifuga the pain increases as the flow increases.

q: Uterine haemorrhage with dark, clotted blood drawn out in long black strings calls for:
why: Dark, stringy, ropy blood is the keynote of Crocus; Ipecac has bright-red blood with nausea.

q: A baby normally begins to smile socially (in response to a face) at about:
why: The social smile appears at 6–8 weeks; it is a key early social milestone.

q: A child can copy a circle at about:
why: Copying a circle is a 3-year fine motor skill; a triangle is copied at about 5 years.

q: Jaundice persisting beyond two weeks in an infant with pale clay-coloured stools and dark urine most suggests:
why: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with acholic stools points to biliary atresia, which needs surgery (Kasai) before 8 weeks.

q: The principal immunoglobulin present in colostrum is:
why: Colostrum is rich in secretory IgA, which protects the infant's gut mucosa.

q: The earliest clinical sign of rickets in a young infant is:
why: Craniotabes (ping-pong softening of the skull) appears in early infancy; rosary and limb deformities come later.

q: The most consistent biochemical finding in nutritional rickets is:
why: Alkaline phosphatase rises with osteoblastic activity; phosphate is low and PTH high.

q: Under the national programme, the first dose of vitamin A given at 9 months of age is:
why: The first dose is 1 lakh IU at 9 months with MR; later doses are 2 lakh IU every 6 months up to 5 years.

q: Under IMNCI, fast breathing in a child aged 2 to 12 months is a respiratory rate of:
why: Cut-offs are 60/min under 2 months, 50/min for 2–12 months and 40/min for 1–5 years.

q: A 'thumb sign' on a lateral neck X-ray of a toxic, drooling child is diagnostic of:
why: The swollen epiglottis appears as a thumb; croup shows a steeple sign on an AP view.

q: The commonest cause of acute bronchiolitis in infants is:
why: RSV causes the majority of bronchiolitis in children under two.

q: A hurried, restless, destructive child who cannot keep still and is better from music needs:
why: Extreme restlessness and hurry with amelioration from music is the keynote of Tarentula hispanica.

q: Bed-wetting in an irritable child who picks at the nose, grinds the teeth in sleep and has a canine hunger calls for:
why: Cina is the classic worm remedy with nose-boring, teeth grinding, ravenous hunger and nocturnal enuresis.

q: Very painful dentition in which the teeth decay as soon as they appear calls for:
why: Kreosotum is noted for painful dentition with rapid decay of the teeth soon after eruption.

q: The pentavalent vaccine in India's UIP protects against diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus and:
opts: hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b
why: Pentavalent = DPT + Hep B + Hib, given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks.

q: Under the UIP, rotavirus vaccine is given:
why: Rotavirus vaccine is an oral vaccine given with the three primary doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks.

q: Under the current UIP, fractional IPV (fIPV, 0.1 mL intradermal) is given at:
why: Since 2023 a third fIPV dose at 9 months has been added to the 6- and 14-week doses.

q: Under the UIP, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) is given as:
opts: three primary doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks with no booster
one dose at birth and a booster at 9 months
one dose at 9 months and a booster at 16–24 months
two primary doses at 6 and 14 weeks and a booster at 9 months
why: India uses a 2+1 PCV schedule: 6 weeks, 14 weeks and a booster at 9–12 months.

q: The second booster of DPT vaccine under the UIP is given at:
why: DPT booster-1 is at 16–24 months and booster-2 at 5–6 years; Td follows at 10 and 16 years.

q: For an infant under one month of age, the dose of BCG vaccine is:
why: BCG is given intradermally in the left upper arm: 0.05 mL up to one month of age and 0.1 mL after that.

q: The birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine under the UIP should be given:
opts: any time in the first year
why: Hep B birth dose is effective in preventing perinatal transmission only if given within 24 hours.

q: A full-thickness (third-degree) burn is typically:
opts: moist and pink with intact sensation
why: Full-thickness burns destroy the nerve endings, so the area is insensate, white or charred and leathery.

q: Curling's ulcer is an acute stress ulcer of the stomach or duodenum seen after:
why: Curling's ulcer follows major burns; Cushing's ulcer follows head injury or raised intracranial pressure.

q: Marjolin's ulcer is a malignant change in a long-standing scar or chronic ulcer, and is histologically a:
why: Marjolin's ulcer is a slow-growing squamous cell carcinoma arising in burn scars or chronic ulcers.

q: A rodent ulcer is a:
why: Rodent ulcer is the common name for basal cell carcinoma, which locally erodes tissue.

q: An ulcer with a punched-out edge, as if cut with a punch, is typical of a:
why: Punched-out edges are seen in gummatous (and trophic) ulcers; TB is undermined, SCC everted, BCC rolled.

q: A painless ulcer over the heel or the head of the first metatarsal in a patient with diabetic or leprotic neuropathy is a:
why: Loss of sensation over pressure points leads to painless perforating trophic ulcers.

q: The basic treatment of an established abscess is:
why: 'Where there is pus, let it out': pus must be drained; antibiotics alone do not penetrate an abscess cavity.

q: Hilton's method of draining an abscess in the axilla or neck involves:
opts: deep sharp incision straight into the cavity
incising the skin and opening the cavity with blunt sinus forceps
complete excision of the abscess wall
why: Blunt opening after a skin incision avoids injury to the important vessels and nerves nearby.

q: In healing by second intention, closure of the wound gap is helped chiefly by:
opts: fibrin glue formed in the first hour
why: Large open wounds fill with granulation tissue and shrink through myofibroblast contraction.

q: A fully immunised adult whose last tetanus dose was 7 years ago has a dirty, tetanus-prone wound. He needs:
opts: a full three-dose course of tetanus toxoid with immunoglobulin
no prophylaxis, as he is fully immunised
why: For a tetanus-prone wound more than 5 years after the last dose, a booster is given; TIG is reserved for incomplete or unknown immunisation.

q: Under standard pre-anaesthetic fasting guidelines for an elective adult operation, clear fluids may be taken up to:
why: Usual rules: clear fluids 2 h, breast milk 4 h, light meal or non-human milk 6 h.

q: The commonest cause of fever in the first 24–48 hours after an abdominal operation is:
why: Early postoperative fever is usually pulmonary collapse; wound infection appears around days 5–7.

q: A Smith's fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with:
opts: volar (anterior) displacement of the distal fragment
dorsal displacement of the distal fragment
fracture of the ulnar styloid only
why: Smith's fracture is the 'reversed Colles'', caused by a fall on the back of the flexed wrist.

q: The commonest bone fractured during birth is the:
why: Clavicle fracture is the most frequent birth fracture, often in shoulder dystocia.

q: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on the outstretched hand suggests a fracture of the scaphoid, whose feared complication is:
opts: avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment
why: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally, so the proximal pole may lose its supply and necrose.

q: In posterior dislocation of the hip, the limb is held in:
why: Posterior dislocation (dashboard injury) gives flexion, adduction and internal rotation, and may injure the sciatic nerve.

q: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a classic complication of:
opts: supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children
fracture of the shaft of the femur
why: Brachial artery injury or compression in supracondylar fracture causes forearm muscle ischaemia and contracture.

q: The earliest and most reliable sign of an impending compartment syndrome is:
opts: severe pain on passive stretching of the muscles
why: Pain out of proportion and on passive stretch comes first; loss of pulse is a late sign.

q: In chronic osteomyelitis, a piece of dead bone separated from living bone is called the:
why: The sequestrum is dead bone; the involucrum is new bone around it; cloacae are openings in the involucrum.

q: Bouchard's nodes in osteoarthritis are found at the:
why: Bouchard's nodes are PIP osteophytes; Heberden's nodes are at the DIP joints.

q: Pain down the leg reproduced when the extended leg is raised from the couch suggests:
opts: lumbar disc prolapse with nerve root compression
why: A positive straight-leg-raising test indicates tension on a compressed L5 or S1 root, usually from a prolapsed disc.

q: The first-aid management of an acute ankle sprain is summed up as:
opts: rest and hot fomentation for a week
why: RICE reduces bleeding and swelling in the first 48–72 hours.

q: When splinting a suspected fracture of a long bone in first aid, the splint should immobilise:
opts: only the joint below the fracture
the whole body on a stretcher in every case
the joint above and the joint below the fracture
why: Immobilising the joints on both sides prevents movement of the fragments.

q: In adults, the paranasal sinus most commonly involved in sinusitis is the:
why: The maxillary sinus is most often affected in adults; the ethmoids are most often affected in children.

q: The commonest bacterial cause of acute otitis media is:
why: S. pneumoniae, then H. influenzae and Moraxella, cause most AOM; Pseudomonas and Proteus are typical of CSOM.

q: The 'unsafe' (atticoantral) type of chronic suppurative otitis media is dangerous mainly because of:
opts: a central perforation of the pars tensa
why: Cholesteatoma in the attic erodes bone and leads to intracranial and extracranial complications.

q: Secondary haemorrhage after tonsillectomy usually occurs:
opts: within 24 hours, due to slipped ligature
5–10 days after operation, due to infection
why: Secondary haemorrhage follows sepsis of the tonsillar fossa around the 5th–10th day; reactionary haemorrhage is within 24 hours.

q: Trachoma, a cause of blindness through conjunctival scarring, is caused by:
why: Serotypes A–C of Chlamydia trachomatis cause trachoma with follicles, Herbert's pits and trichiasis.

q: The normal range of intraocular pressure is about:
why: Normal IOP is 10–21 mm Hg; persistent values above this raise suspicion of glaucoma.

q: Which eye drop is contraindicated in a patient with a shallow anterior chamber and narrow angles?
why: Mydriatics such as atropine can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma; pilocarpine is used to treat it.

q: Conjunctivitis with profuse, acrid, burning tears but a bland nasal discharge calls for:
why: Euphrasia has acrid lachrymation with bland coryza, the reverse of Allium cepa.

q: Sinusitis with thick, tough, stringy, yellow-green discharge and pain at the root of the nose calls for:
why: Ropy, stringy discharge with pressure pain at the root of the nose is the keynote of Kali bichromicum.

q: Called the 'homoeopathic knife' for its power to hasten suppuration in whitlow and abscess, the remedy is:
why: Myristica sebifera hastens suppuration and is often said to shorten the course of panaritium.

q: Deep bruising of soft tissues such as the breasts, pelvic organs or abdominal wall after injury or surgery calls for:
why: Bellis perennis acts on deep tissue trauma, especially of the trunk, breasts and pelvic organs.

q: Acute fright and fear of death immediately after an accident, with great anxiety and restlessness, calls for:
why: Aconite suits sudden, violent shock with intense fear of death.

q: Burns and scalds with intense, raw, smarting pain, before or after blisters form, call for:
why: Cantharis is the leading remedy for burns with violent burning pains and vesication.

q: Mental symptoms such as depression or irritability arising as ill effects of a head injury call for:
why: Natrum sulph is known for chronic mental effects of injuries to the head.

q: Retention of flatus with distension after abdominal operations, with no passage of gas up or down, calls for:
why: Raphanus is the noted remedy for postoperative gas retention.

q: The first aid to stop external bleeding from a limb wound is:
opts: washing the wound with hot water
applying a cold drink to the lips
firm direct pressure over the wound with a clean pad
why: Direct pressure with elevation stops most external haemorrhage; a tourniquet is a last resort.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of India's 'Big Four' venomous snakes?
why: The Big Four are the spectacled cobra, common krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper.

q: After a snakebite, blood that fails to clot in the 20-minute whole blood clotting test indicates envenomation by a:
why: Viper venom is haemotoxic and causes coagulopathy; cobra and krait venoms are neurotoxic.

q: The specific antidote for paracetamol overdose is:
why: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and prevents liver necrosis.

q: In kerosene poisoning, inducing vomiting is avoided chiefly because it may cause:
why: The main danger of hydrocarbons is aspiration into the lungs, causing chemical pneumonitis.

q: For a conscious adult who is choking and cannot speak or cough, the recommended first aid is:
opts: a blind finger sweep of the throat
laying the person flat and waiting
why: Back blows and abdominal thrusts dislodge the obstruction; blind finger sweeps are avoided.

q: The first aid for an animal bite with suspected rabies exposure is to:
opts: suture the wound tightly at once
wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
cover it with a tight bandage without washing
why: Thorough washing removes much of the virus; the wound is not sutured early, and vaccine with or without RIG follows.

q: The secondary attack rate is mainly a measure of:
opts: the case fatality of a disease
the infectiousness (communicability) of a disease among susceptible contacts
the virulence of the agent in the index case
the total burden of disease in the community
why: Secondary attack rate = cases among contacts within one incubation period / susceptible contacts; Park uses it to measure communicability.

q: In a common-source, single-exposure (point-source) epidemic, the epidemic curve typically shows:
opts: several waves separated by one serial interval each
a slow rise lasting many incubation periods
a steady level of cases over years
a sharp rise and fall, with all cases occurring within one incubation period
why: A point-source outbreak (e.g. food poisoning) clusters within one incubation period with no secondary waves; propagated epidemics show gradual rise and successive waves.

q: In a cohort study, the incidence of lung cancer among smokers minus that among non-smokers gives the:
why: Attributable risk is the difference in incidence between exposed and non-exposed; it shows how much disease could be prevented by removing the exposure. Relative risk is the ratio.

q: Preventing the emergence of risk factors (such as unhealthy diets) in a population where they have not yet appeared is called:
why: Primordial prevention acts before risk factors arise, mainly by health education and lifestyle change in children.

q: A screening test gives: true positives 80, false negatives 20, false positives 30, true negatives 870. Its sensitivity is:
why: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) = 80/100 = 80%. 72.7% is the PPV, 96.7% the specificity and 97.8% the NPV.

q: According to the Organon, the complete symptom picture of a prevailing epidemic disease (for the genus epidemicus) is obtained by:
opts: studying the first patient only, as he shows the purest symptoms
consulting the remedy used in the previous epidemic of the same name
noting only the pathological diagnosis common to all patients
careful observation of several cases, since each patient shows only part of the whole picture
why: Organon §§100-102: each epidemic is treated as new, and the totality is gathered from several cases, as one patient presents only a portion of it.

q: In the Asiatic cholera epidemic of 1831, the remedy Hahnemann advised for the first stage was:
why: Hahnemann advised Camphor in the first stage and Cuprum or Veratrum album in the later stages of cholera.

q: In 2020 the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP) was renamed the:
opts: National Programme for Control of Tuberculosis
why: RNTCP became NTEP in 2020, reflecting the goal of eliminating TB.

q: Under the National Leprosy Eradication Programme, a patient with six or more skin lesions is classified as:
why: Under NLEP, 1-5 skin lesions is paucibacillary and 6 or more lesions (or a positive smear) is multibacillary.

q: In the 95-95-95 target of the National AIDS Control Programme, the second '95' refers to:
opts: 95% of people with HIV knowing their status
95% of people on treatment having viral suppression
95% of people diagnosed with HIV receiving sustained antiretroviral therapy
why: The cascade is 95% diagnosed, 95% of the diagnosed on ART, and 95% of those on ART virally suppressed.

q: The population norm for one Primary Health Centre in hilly, tribal or difficult areas is:
why: A PHC covers 30,000 in plains and 20,000 in hilly or tribal areas; 80,000 is the CHC norm for hilly areas.

q: Under Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), children are screened for defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and:
why: RBSK screens children aged 0-18 years for the '4 Ds': defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays including disability.

q: The sex ratio of India in the 2011 Census was:
why: Census 2011 recorded 943; 919 was the child (0-6) sex ratio and 933 the 2001 figure.

q: The dependency ratio is calculated as:
opts: population aged 65 and above / total population
why: The dependency ratio relates the economically dependent young and old to the working-age population of 15-64 years.

q: A net reproduction rate (NRR) of 1 means that:
opts: each woman bears exactly one child
the population is doubling every generation
each generation of mothers is exactly replaced by an equal number of daughters
the birth rate equals 1 per 1,000 population
why: NRR = 1 is replacement-level fertility, roughly equal to a TFR of about 2.1.

q: The denominator of the perinatal mortality rate is:
opts: live births plus still births in the year
why: Perinatal mortality rate = (still births of 28 weeks or more + deaths in the first 7 days) per 1,000 live births plus still births.

q: Haemoglobin in a large adult sample is normally distributed with mean 12 g/dL and standard deviation 1 g/dL. About what proportion lies between 10 and 14 g/dL?
why: 10-14 is mean +/- 2 SD, which covers about 95% of a normal distribution; +/- 1 SD covers 68%.

q: To test whether the proportion of smokers differs between men and women, the appropriate test is the:
why: Chi-square compares proportions (qualitative data); t-tests and ANOVA compare means.

q: A type I (alpha) error in hypothesis testing is:
opts: rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true
accepting a null hypothesis that is actually false
why: Type I error is a false positive conclusion (rejecting a true null hypothesis); accepting a false null hypothesis is a type II error.

q: In a slow sand filter, the 'vital layer' that does the purification is called the:
why: The Schmutzdecke, a slimy layer of algae, bacteria and plankton on the sand surface, is the heart of the slow sand filter.

q: Horrock's apparatus is used to find:
opts: the dose of bleaching powder needed to disinfect well water
why: Horrock's apparatus estimates the amount of bleaching powder needed to give a free residual chlorine in water.

q: The Nalgonda technique is used for:
opts: removal of excess fluoride from drinking water
why: Developed by NEERI, the Nalgonda technique uses alum and lime to defluoridate water; fluoride above 1.5 mg/L causes fluorosis.

q: Under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, used hypodermic needles and scalpel blades go into the:
why: Sharps, including needles, syringes with fixed needles and blades, go into the white translucent puncture-proof container.

q: According to Nysten's rule, rigor mortis passes off:
opts: in the reverse order of its appearance
all over the body at the same time
in the same order in which it appeared
why: Rigor appears in eyelids, face, neck, trunk, upper then lower limbs, and passes off in the same sequence.

q: According to Casper's dictum, the putrefaction seen in a body after one week in air equals that seen after:
opts: two weeks in water and eight weeks in earth
one week in water and two weeks in earth
eight weeks in water and two weeks in earth
four weeks in water and four weeks in earth
why: Casper's dictum gives rates of decomposition in air, water and earth as 1 : 2 : 8 (in terms of time to equal change).

q: Adipocere formation results from:
opts: drying of tissues in hot, dry air
hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fat in warm, moist conditions
freezing of body water in cold climates
why: Adipocere (saponification) is the conversion of fat into a soapy waxy substance in warm, moist surroundings; drying in hot air causes mummification.

q: Tissue bridges, ragged margins and bruised edges in a wound indicate a:
why: A laceration is a tear from blunt force, leaving nerves and vessels as tissue bridges; incised wounds have clean edges.

q: Multiple superficial, parallel cuts at the start of a deeper incised wound on the wrist are called hesitation cuts and suggest:
why: Hesitation (tentative) cuts reflect a trial before the final cut and are typical of suicidal incised wounds.

q: A firearm entry wound is characterised by:
opts: everted margins without an abrasion collar
a wound larger than the exit wound in all cases
inverted margins with an abrasion collar
why: Entry wounds are small with inverted edges and an abrasion (contusion) collar; exit wounds are usually larger and everted, without a collar.

q: Fracture of the hyoid bone is most commonly seen in death by:
why: Hyoid fracture is commonest in throttling because of direct finger pressure on the neck (Reddy).

q: Diatoms found in the bone marrow of a body recovered from water indicate:
opts: the body was thrown into water after death
death by head injury before immersion
the body remained in water for over one week
why: Diatoms reach the marrow only through the circulation of a living person inhaling water, so they prove ante-mortem drowning.

q: Convulsions with opisthotonus and risus sardonicus, with the mind clear between the fits, suggest poisoning by:
why: Strychnine blocks glycine inhibition in the spinal cord, causing tetanic convulsions while consciousness is preserved between fits.

q: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023, hurt that causes severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits is grievous when it lasts for at least:
why: BNS section 116 reduced the period from the 20 days of IPC 320 to 15 days.

q: The police inquest, formerly under CrPC section 174, is now covered by:
why: BNSS 194 replaces CrPC 174 (police inquest); BNSS 196 replaces CrPC 176 (magistrate inquest).

q: A blue line along the gum margins (Burtonian line) is a sign of chronic poisoning by:
why: The Burtonian line is lead sulphide deposited at the gum margin in chronic lead poisoning.

q: The 'Bolam test' in medical negligence holds that a doctor is not negligent if:
opts: the patient had signed a written consent form
he acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of fellow practitioners
the outcome of the treatment was favourable
he had charged no fee for the treatment
why: Bolam v. Friern Hospital (1957): the standard of care is that of a responsible body of skilled practitioners in that field.

q: In Poonam Verma v. Ashwin Patel (1996), the Supreme Court held that a homoeopath prescribing allopathic drugs without the required qualification is:
opts: protected under the Consumer Protection Act
guilty only if the patient dies
not negligent if the drug is commonly used
why: Practising a system of medicine without qualification in it was held to be negligence per se.

q: In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005), the Supreme Court held that to prosecute a doctor for criminal negligence:
opts: any error of judgement is enough
the negligence must be gross or reckless, and a private complaint should be supported by a credible medical opinion
the patient's consent form must be produced first
only a civil suit for compensation is permitted
why: The judgment set guidelines protecting doctors from frivolous criminal prosecution: simple lack of care is civil; criminal liability needs gross negligence.

q: Sharing of fees between a referring doctor and a consultant without the patient's knowledge is called:
why: Fee-splitting (dichotomy) is infamous conduct; covering is shielding an unqualified person.

q: The Declaration of Helsinki (1964) of the World Medical Association deals with:
opts: ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects
the determination of the time of death
why: Helsinki covers research on human subjects; Tokyo (1975) torture, Sydney (1968) death, Geneva (1948) the oath.

q: The ethical principle expressed as 'primum non nocere' is:
why: Primum non nocere ('first, do no harm') is the principle of non-maleficence.

q: A patient enters a clinic and holds out his arm when asked to. This implied consent is valid for:
opts: any procedure the doctor thinks fit
why: Implied consent covers only general examination; procedures with risk, and intimate examinations, need expressed (preferably written) consent.

q: Regarding a dying declaration recorded by a doctor, which statement is correct?
opts: The accused must be present and may cross-examine
It is valid only if recorded by a magistrate
It must be made in the presence of a police officer
No oath is given, and the doctor should certify that the declarant was conscious and of sound mind
why: A dying declaration needs no oath and no presence of the accused; the doctor certifies compos mentis. The dying deposition, with the accused present, is recorded by a magistrate.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the autonomous boards constituted under the National Commission for Homoeopathy Act, 2020?
opts: Medical Assessment and Rating Board for Homoeopathy
Board of Ethics and Registration for Homoeopathy
why: The NCH Act sets up three autonomous boards: Education, Medical Assessment and Rating, and Ethics and Registration; pharmacopoeia work lies outside it.

q: Sex determination of a foetus is prohibited in India under the:
why: The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994 (amended 2003) bans sex selection and sex determination.
